publicQuestions.question:
Thank you for the clarifications provided in Addendum No. 1. Following our review of the tender package and information covered in Addendum No. 1, could Council please clarify the following matters?

1. Submission for an individual work package

The RFQ permits Council to award the work packages separately. Can Council confirm that respondents may submit a quotation for the Parks and Open Space work package only, or the Bridge work package only?

2. Payment for additional open space assets

The fee schedule provides a lump sum for the assets listed in Appendix 1 and a schedule-of-rates item for additional new/found/missing assets.

Can Council confirm that additional assets will be paid at the accepted schedule of rates, separately from the base lump sum, and advise the required approval and reconciliation process? Please also confirm whether respondents may provide rates by asset type and appropriate unit of measurement.

3. Open space renewal costs and valuation requirements

Appendix 1, section 8, Table 5 includes “Renewal Cost” as a required field.

Can Council confirm whether this requirement is limited to indicative renewal/replacement costs for asset planning, or whether the consultant must undertake an asset valuation in accordance with applicable Australian Accounting Standards, including AASB 13, for financial reporting purposes?

If a financial reporting valuation is required, please confirm the valuation date, required outputs and report, applicable Council valuation policies, and whether liaison with Council’s Finance team and external auditors is included.

If indicative renewal/replacement costs only are required, will Council provide adopted unit rates and costing assumptions, or should the consultant develop these? Please confirm whether Addendum No. 1, question 11, also applies to open space assets.

4. Open space scope boundaries

For playground equipment, fitness equipment and park lighting, can Council confirm whether the requirement is a visual inventory and condition assessment, or whether any specialist safety/compliance inspection or functional testing is required?

5. Konect configuration and systems administration

Appendix 1 indicates that Council will set up Konect and that its GIS Administrator will assist with configuration.

Can Council clarify the division of responsibility between Council and the consultant for initial configuration and ongoing systems administration, including:

•	Asset layers, forms, mandatory fields and pick lists.

•	User accounts, permissions and licences.

•	Asset and defect identifiers and relationships.

•	Configuration changes identified during the pilot or subsequent fieldwork.

•	Synchronisation issues, technical support and data recovery.

Please confirm whether Council will provide all necessary Konect licences and user accounts at no cost to the consultant.

6. Konect training and induction

Will Council provide training or induction in its specific Konect configuration, data collection workflows and business rules?

If so, please advise the anticipated duration, delivery format, personnel required to attend and whether respondents should include this attendance time in their fee and program.

7. Konect Manager access and quality assurance

Will the successful consultant receive Konect Manager access, with sufficient permissions to review, query and export asset and defect data and photograph references, undertake bulk validation and complete its own QA processes?

Please clarify whether the consultant may correct data through Konect Manager or approved bulk updates. If access is restricted, what arrangements will Council provide to enable timely QA, correction and verification before final submission?

8. Pilot and repeatability acceptance

Further to Addendum No. 1, question 8, we understand that condition ratings must match Council’s ratings for more than 95% of sampled assets.

Could Council please confirm:

•	Whether the approximately 2% pilot and 7% repeatability sample are measured by asset numbers, site numbers or both.

•	The acceptance tolerances for attribute data and dimensions.

•	How the extent of reassessment will be determined if the repeatability threshold is not achieved.

•	The anticipated turnaround for pilot review and approval.

9. Spatial accuracy

The collection manual discusses ±1 m positioning as an industry standard, while Addendum No. 1, question 4, specifies suitable devices without defining positional accuracy.

Can Council confirm the required horizontal accuracy and acceptance method for asset locations and mapped extents, including whether positioning against Council’s aerial imagery is acceptable where GPS reception is restricted?

10. Immediate safety risks

Appendix 1, section 10.3 requires reasonable steps to protect the public where a serious or immediate safety risk is identified.

Can Council confirm the required notification and escalation process, and whether inspectors are expected to undertake any physical intervention, such as installing barriers or hazard markers, beyond reporting the risk?

11. Bridge access and inspection limitations

Addendum No. 1, question 13, confirms that Level 3 inspections and load rating are excluded, but does not expressly address the other access activities included in the question.

Can Council confirm whether confined-space entry, underwater inspections and specialist access equipment are required for this commission? Where these activities are necessary to complete the required inspection, should they be included in the lump sum or treated as separately authorised additional services?

12. Previous bridge reports and reporting requirements

Will previous inspection reports and defect records for all 73 structures be provided to the successful consultant to support comparison with the new inspection findings?

Can Council also confirm whether the Binnak Park sample report represents the required reporting format, and provide the method for deriving the overall five-point structure rating from the component condition assessments?

13. Insurance requirements

Special Conditions amendment 2.42 requires public liability insurance to name both Council and the consultant as insureds. Annexure A Item 28 also lists insurances to be effected by the Client.

Can Council clarify the intended insurance responsibilities and confirm whether noting Council’s interest on the consultant’s public liability policy would satisfy the requirement, or whether joint-insured status is required?

14. Contract documents and payment terms

The RFQ refers to purchase order terms, while the tender package includes an amended AS4122 consultancy agreement. The RFQ also states 30-day payment terms, whereas Annexure A Item 11 specifies 20 business days.

Can Council confirm the applicable payment period?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Submission for an individual work package

The RFQ permits Council to award the work packages separately. Can Council confirm that respondents may submit a quotation for the Parks and Open Space work package only, or the Bridge work package only?

Council Response: Yes. This was also addressed by previous questions. Please ensure you review other questions and responses posted.

2. Payment for additional open space assets

The fee schedule provides a lump sum for the assets listed in Appendix 1 and a schedule-of-rates item for additional new/found/missing assets.

Can Council confirm that additional assets will be paid at the accepted schedule of rates, separately from the base lump sum, and advise the required approval and reconciliation process? Please also confirm whether respondents may provide rates by asset type and appropriate unit of measurement.

Council Response: Yes. Council will pay for additional assets at the accepted schedule of rates, separately from the base lump sum. Respondents are required to provide rates by asset type and the appropriate unit of measurement.

3. Open space renewal costs and valuation requirements

Appendix 1, section 8, Table 5 includes “Renewal Cost” as a required field.

Can Council confirm whether this requirement is limited to indicative renewal/replacement costs for asset planning, or whether the consultant must undertake an asset valuation in accordance with applicable Australian Accounting Standards, including AASB 13, for financial reporting purposes?

Council Response: Council requires indicative renewal/replacement costs for asset management and future renewal planning purposes only. A formal asset valuation for financial reporting purposes, including valuation in accordance with AASB 13, is not required.

If a financial reporting valuation is required, please confirm the valuation date, required outputs and report, applicable Council valuation policies, and whether liaison with Council’s Finance team and external auditors is included.

If indicative renewal/replacement costs only are required, will Council provide adopted unit rates and costing assumptions, or should the consultant develop these? Please confirm whether Addendum No. 1, question 11, also applies to open space assets.

Council Response: Council will not provide unit rates or costing assumptions. The consultant is responsible for developing appropriate costs using industry-standard unit rates.

4. Open space scope boundaries

For playground equipment, fitness equipment and park lighting, can Council confirm whether the requirement is a visual inventory and condition assessment, or whether any specialist safety/compliance inspection or functional testing is required?

Council Response: A visual inventory and condition assessment are sufficient. Specialist safety/compliance inspections and functional testing are not required.

5. Konect configuration and systems administration

Appendix 1 indicates that Council will set up Konect and that its GIS Administrator will assist with configuration.

Can Council clarify the division of responsibility between Council and the consultant for initial configuration and ongoing systems administration, including:

• Asset layers, forms, mandatory fields and pick lists.

• User accounts, permissions and licences.

• Asset and defect identifiers and relationships.

• Configuration changes identified during the pilot or subsequent fieldwork.

• Synchronisation issues, technical support and data recovery.

Please confirm whether Council will provide all necessary Konect licences and user accounts at no cost to the consultant.

Council Response: Council will undertake the initial Konect setup and configuration as required and will remain responsible for ongoing system administration. This includes managing system configuration, user accounts, permissions, licences and any necessary technical support.

Council will provide the required Konect licences and user accounts to the successful consultant at no cost.

6. Konect training and induction

Will Council provide training or induction in its specific Konect configuration, data collection workflows and business rules?

If so, please advise the anticipated duration, delivery format, personnel required to attend and whether respondents should include this attendance time in their fee and program.

Council Response: Yes. Council is happy to provide an induction covering the Konect configuration and relevant data collection workflows. The anticipated duration is approximately one hour. Respondents should allow for this induction in their project program and fee.

7. Konect Manager access and quality assurance

Will the successful consultant receive Konect Manager access, with sufficient permissions to review, query and export asset and defect data and photograph references, undertake bulk validation and complete its own QA processes?

Please clarify whether the consultant may correct data through Konect Manager or approved bulk updates. If access is restricted, what arrangements will Council provide to enable timely QA, correction and verification before final submission?

Council Response: The consultant will not be provided with Konect Manager access. Council will provide relevant asset and defect data upon request to support the consultant's quality assurance and validation processes.

Data corrections and updates will be managed through Council's agreed processes. Bulk data updates by the consultant are not applicable.

8. Pilot and repeatability acceptance

Further to Addendum No. 1, question 8, we understand that condition ratings must match Council’s ratings for more than 95% of sampled assets.

Could Council please confirm:

• Whether the approximately 2% pilot and 7% repeatability sample are measured by asset numbers, site numbers or both.

• The acceptance tolerances for attribute data and dimensions.

• How the extent of reassessment will be determined if the repeatability threshold is not achieved.

• The anticipated turnaround for pilot review and approval.

Council Response:

•	The approximately 2% pilot and 7% repeatability samples will be measured by the number of sites.

•	All asset attributes are to be captured and checked as part of the audit. Dimensional measurements must achieve an accuracy of greater than 98%. For example, a measured length of 100 metres must be within the range of 98 to 102 metres.

•	If the required repeatability threshold is not achieved, the consultant will be required to review and update the methodology and condition ratings as necessary.

•	Council anticipates a review and approval timeframe of approximately two weeks for the pilot.

9. Spatial accuracy

The collection manual discusses ±1 m positioning as an industry standard, while Addendum No. 1, question 4, specifies suitable devices without defining positional accuracy.

Can Council confirm the required horizontal accuracy and acceptance method for asset locations and mapped extents, including whether positioning against Council’s aerial imagery is acceptable where GPS reception is restricted?

Council Response: Asset locations and mapped extents will not be collected using GPS devices. The consultant will identify and record asset locations and extents through direct interaction with the map within the Konect system.

10. Immediate safety risks

Appendix 1, section 10.3 requires reasonable steps to protect the public where a serious or immediate safety risk is identified.

Can Council confirm the required notification and escalation process, and whether inspectors are expected to undertake any physical intervention, such as installing barriers or hazard markers, beyond reporting the risk?

Council Response: Where an inspector identifies a serious or immediate safety risk, they must promptly notify Council. Council will assess the reported risk and arrange the necessary actions to protect public safety. Inspectors are not expected to undertake physical intervention, such as installing barriers or hazard markers.

11. Bridge access and inspection limitations

Addendum No. 1, question 13, confirms that Level 3 inspections and load rating are excluded, but does not expressly address the other access activities included in the question.

Can Council confirm whether confined-space entry, underwater inspections and specialist access equipment are required for this commission? Where these activities are necessary to complete the required inspection, should they be included in the lump sum or treated as separately authorised additional services?

Council Response: Council has not encountered the need for confined-space entry, underwater inspections or specialist access equipment during previous bridge condition audits. However, should any such requirements arise during the project, the consultant should discuss the matter with Council to clarify the requirements and agree on an appropriate approach before proceeding.

12. Previous bridge reports and reporting requirements

Will previous inspection reports and defect records for all 73 structures be provided to the successful consultant to support comparison with the new inspection findings?

Can Council also confirm whether the Binnak Park sample report represents the required reporting format, and provide the method for deriving the overall five-point structure rating from the component condition assessments?

Council Response: Council will not provide all previous inspection reports and defect records for the 73 structures. However, Council may provide selected previous inspection reports as samples where appropriate.

The Binnak Park sample report is provided as a guide only. Council is open to accepting alternative reporting formats, provided they adequately address the project requirements and deliver the required inspection information and outcomes.

13. Insurance requirements

Special Conditions amendment 2.42 requires public liability insurance to name both Council and the consultant as insureds. Annexure A Item 28 also lists insurances to be effected by the Client.

Can Council clarify the intended insurance responsibilities and confirm whether noting Council’s interest on the consultant’s public liability policy would satisfy the requirement, or whether joint-insured status is required?

Council Response: This has not been previously raised. Generally insurances received are in the tendering companies name but please indicate your concern in your submission.

14. Contract documents and payment terms

The RFQ refers to purchase order terms, while the tender package includes an amended AS4122 consultancy agreement. The RFQ also states 30-day payment terms, whereas Annexure A Item 11 specifies 20 business days.

Can Council confirm the applicable payment period?

Council Response: This has not been previously raised. Please assume Council std payment terms of 30 days and the issue will be resolved with the successful contractor and an internal review of the documents undertaken to resolve for future contracts.

For a parks-only submission, could Council confirm which of these assets remain within the parks package and which are covered by the separate bridge package? Could an exclusion list or asset IDs be provided to avoid omissions or duplication between the two contracts?

Bridges and boardwalks are not included in the parks-only submission.

Asset IDs will be available in the Konect dataset to be provided after awarding the contract.

Council response: Asset IDs will be available in the Konect dataset provided following contract award. Most asset type-related attributes are detailed in Appendix 1A – Open Space Assets and Attributes Matrix. For any attributes not covered in the appendix, the awarded consultant can refer to the Konect dataset for further information.

4. Approval and reconciliation of additional assets

Could Council confirm how additional assets will be approved and reconciled for payment? In particular, is approval required before collecting their full details, or can newly identified assets be captured during the survey and submitted in an agreed reconciliation register?

Council response: Newly identified assets can be captured during the survey and submitted in an agreed reconciliation register for Council review and approval. Prior approval is not required before collecting their full details. Any additional assets identified through the survey will be assessed and reconciled as part of the agreed variation and payment process.

5. Data access and quality assurance

We acknowledge that Konect Manager and Manager Lite access will not be provided.

Could Council confirm the expected turnaround for requested data exports and corrections, and whether a regular export schedule can be agreed to support ongoing quality checks?

If the repeatability threshold is not met, how will Council determine the extent of reassessment—for example, whether this applies to sampled sites, affected asset types or a broader portion of the survey?

Council response: Regular scheduling of data export will not be an issue. It can be provided as requested.

6. Map positioning accuracy

We understand that locations and mapped extents will be recorded directly on the map in Konect rather than through GPS capture.

Could Council confirm the positional accuracy or acceptance criteria that will apply, including the approach where assets are obscured in aerial imagery?

Council response: The operator's best interpretation, given the use of aerial photography, with aid from the current location shown by location services, should enable accuracy sufficient for Council's needs.

7. Applicable parks manual

The parks specification references a June 2021 manual, while the supplied manual records a September 2023 creation and endorsement date.

Could Council confirm that the supplied September 2023 manual is the applicable version, subject to the project specification and subsequent tender clarifications?

Council response: Council is confirming that the supplied September 2023 manual is the applicable version, subject to the project specification and subsequent tender clarifications.

To ensure our submission accurately identifies any departure, could Council confirm whether noting Council’s interest on our public liability policy would be acceptable, or whether Council must be named as a joint insured under Special Conditions amendment 2.42? Please also confirm whether MCC’s nominated Ecologist is required to undertake the associated ecological services, including pre-clearing and post-clearing reporting, Flora and Fauna Management Plan/Clearing and Grubbing Plan input, fauna relocation, microbat inspections and Manning River Helmeted Turtle inspections, or whether the Contractor may engage its own suitably qualified ecologist for these services.
publicQuestions.answer:
The Contractor is responsible for engaging and paying for its own suitably qualified ecologist to undertake the ecological services required by the Specifications and the Review of Environmental Factors (REF).

References to the “MCC Ecologist” in G40 Clause 2.4 are to be interpreted as the Contractor's suitably qualified ecologist. The Contractor is not required to engage a particular ecological consultant nominated by MidCoast Council.

The Contractor must allow for all applicable ecological services, including pre-clearing and post-clearing inspections and reporting, clearing supervision, fauna management and relocation, microbat inspections, Manning River Helmeted Turtle inspections, and input into the relevant environmental management plans.

All services must be undertaken in accordance with the Specifications, REF and applicable statutory requirements.

publicQuestions.question:
G36 Annexure A2 Environmental Management Sub Plans states no requirement for an Aboriginal Heritage Management Plan or Non-Aboriginal Heritage Management Plan but if then denoted with a (2). This notation refers to the opportunity that both of these plans may be combined together into Heritage Management Sub-Plan. Please confirm if any heritage plans are required.

G36 Annexure G36/C Schedule of Hold Points references a hold point for Clause 4.9 for Aboriginal Cultural Heritage Salvage. Please confirm of any heritage salvage is required as this is not specified elsewhere in environmental planning documents.

G36 Annexure G36 C Schedule of Hold Points references a hold point for Clause 4.8.1 for Microbat Management however there is no detail in what is required for this hold point. Please confirm what requirements constitute this hold point.

What is the status of the s200 Fisheries Permit – draft permit has been provided as part of Addendum 02. Is MCC awaiting the Contractor’s methodology to lodge this permit only? What is the expected review/approval time that should be allowed?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Heritage Management Plans

Separate Aboriginal and Non-Aboriginal Heritage Management Sub-Plans are not required. The Contractor must address the applicable heritage requirements, including unexpected finds procedures, within the CEMP in accordance with G36 Clauses 4.9 and 4.10.

2. Aboriginal Heritage Salvage

No Aboriginal heritage salvage works are identified in the REF. The Hold Point under Clause 4.9 in Annexure G36/C will be removed by addendum.

3. Microbat Management

The Microbat Management Hold Point under Clause 4.8.1 in Annexure G36/C is not applicable and will be removed by addendum. The Contractor must comply with the microbat inspection and management requirements of G36 Clause 4.8 and the REF.

4. Fisheries Permit

Council will coordinate the Fisheries permit application for the permanent works and preliminary temporary works, including subsequent approvals required for the Contractor's detailed temporary works.

The Contractor's submission requirements are specified in G36 Clause 3.2.2. Approval timeframes are subject to NSW Fisheries assessment and cannot be guaranteed. The Contractor must allow for the approval process in its construction program.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi Team,

Earthworks Queries:

1.	Topsoil stripping depth (R44P1.1, R178P2). The drawings and the geotechnical report RGS03874.1 don’t nominate a topsoil stripping depth. Please confirm the depth to be adopted outside the existing road footprint, including the hillside terracing areas beneath the project specific rock fill (R44 cl 3.4).

2.	Existing pavement within the works. Drawing 01312 notes that the existing road approaches are to be removed. Please confirm:

1.	That removal of the existing pavement is to be included in R44P2 General Earthworks, as there is no profiling or milling pay item.

2.	What pavement thickness should be assumed

3.	That existing pavement material may be reused as select fill, as allowed in the RGS03874.1 ; section 4.2 ; point 4 recommendations.

Regards,
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Topsoil stripping depth - Remove the full depth of topsoil encountered within the areas requiring stripping, including the embankment foundations and hillside-terracing areas, in accordance with TfNSW R44 Clause 2.5.1.

Include all costs associated with topsoil removal and stockpiling in the Lump Sum under Pay Item R44P1.1. The 50 mm topsoil thickness specified in TfNSW R178 applies to the replacement of topsoil for revegetation and does not define the stripping depth.

2. Existing pavement within the Works

a) Payment for removal - Include removal of the existing pavement within the road-approach Works in the Lump Sum under Pay Item R44P2. No separate profiling or milling Pay Item applies. The Contractor is responsible for selecting its removal methodology.

b) Existing pavement thickness - The Contract Documents do not nominate an existing pavement thickness. Tenderers must make their own assessment based on the information provided and Site conditions. The Lump Sum under Pay Item R44P2 must include removal of the full pavement thickness encountered within the specified removal limits.

 c) Reuse of existing pavement material - Existing granular pavement material may be reused only where the proposed processing methodology and supporting test results demonstrate compliance with TfNSW R44 for its proposed use. Bituminous materials, including asphalt and sprayed seals, and any stabilised material unsuitable for reuse must be separated and managed in accordance with the Contract’s recycling and disposal requirements.

Where retention of existing pavement is permitted by the Contract, it must be prepared in accordance with the Drawings and TfNSW R44, including scarifying or ripping, moisture conditioning and recompaction where applicable. The Contractor remains responsible for determining the appropriate methodology.

title: Network Safeworking Services Panel
description:
Queensland Rail is seeking suitably qualified and experienced suppliers for the establishment of a Network Safeworking Services Panel to provide safeworking personnel across the Queensland Rail network. description:

The preferred approach is permanent in-situ decommissioning because physical removal of the underground tanks is considered not reasonably practicable due to restricted access, excavation depth and the proximity of existing Marketplace structural elements. Where apprentice rates will be included into the relevant trade costs, $0 can be input.

publicQuestions.question:
The Labour Rates schedule provides a Minimum Charge row across the Normal Hours, After Hours, Saturday, Sunday and Public Holiday columns, while the Call-Out & Travel schedule separately provides Standard, After Hours and Emergency Response Call-Out fields.

publicQuestions.question:

2. Yes equipment and materials at cost plus markup is acceptable.

3. Travel and remote allowance rates will be considered in the price evaluation.

publicQuestions.question: Volume 4 has one set of labour rates per respondent. If there is a single rate across all services being applied for, then a single Volume 4 will be fine.

Where varying rates would be applied for differing services, multiple tabs clearly marked with which service the rate relates to, will be preferred.

publicQuestions.question:
Council’s services spreadsheet omits a selectable Multidisciplinary Consultancy category although EOI identifies it. How should respondents nominate category G, and is a companion schedule acceptable?

May a respondent select a subcategory when only a defined structural engineering subset is offered, provided the limitations and specialist interfaces are disclosed in the methodology?

The evaluation criterion refers to category-specific publicly available standard and senior hourly rates, but the supplied workbook has only one pair of rate cells. Should respondents provide one pair overall or one pair per nominated category?

Are the EOI indicative hourly rates assessment-only, with future services priced through project-specific negotiated rates and lump-sum quotations, including travel and specialist disbursements?

How does Council assess regional/office-location contribution for a Melbourne-based specialist that regularly works in adjoining Byron Shire and will use approved local subcontractors?

Can respondents submit the names of intended specialists and state that ABN, formal consent and evidence will be provided if shortlisted, or must each prospective subconsultant be formally committed at EOI close?

For relevant-project value, will Council accept professional-service value as commercial-in-confidence (with a range or on-request disclosure), or is a numeric dollar figure mandatory?

Does Council require the entire Quality, Environmental and WHS management system manuals or are approved policies, plan summaries and sample registers sufficient? Is ISO accreditation optional?

For structural/temporary-works-only services under Roads and Traffic, must respondent hold a separate traffic-management/road safety accreditation, or is it acceptable for the traffic component to be separately subcontracted?

Are interstate engineers eligible for professional design roles subject to applicable NSW registration, and are there specific nominated disciplines/registration categories for this panel?

Are all seven categories intended to be accessible to small specialist firms, or will proposals be assessed against full-service requirements across each nominated category?

Can Council provide its Statement of Business Ethics and confirm acceptable method of signing the Conflict of Interest declaration (electronic signature or signed PDF)?

Will Council provide any standard panel deed, rate escalation provisions and interstate travel/disbursement policy before shortlisted respondents accept appointment?

Does Council intend to request specific local availability or maximum response times for emergency assessment call-outs, and may providers nominate advance mobilisation/lead times?
publicQuestions.answer:
Q1) Council’s services spreadsheet omits a selectable Multidisciplinary Consultancy category although EOI identifies it. How should respondents nominate category G, and is a companion schedule acceptable?

A1) Respondents can provide details of any multidisciplinary services as a separate submission.

Q2) May a respondent select a subcategory when only a defined structural engineering subset is offered, provided the limitations and specialist interfaces are disclosed in the methodology?

A2) Yes.

Q3) The evaluation criterion refers to category-specific publicly available standard and senior hourly rates, but the supplied workbook has only one pair of rate cells. Should respondents provide one pair overall or one pair per nominated category?

A3) Respondents should provide their highest senior and standard hourly rate for all, rather than each, categories. It will be considered as an indicative gauge of a respondents competitiveness.

Q4) Are the EOI indicative hourly rates assessment-only, with future services priced through project-specific negotiated rates and lump-sum quotations, including travel and specialist disbursements?

A4) Assessment only. Pricing will be requested and provided per separate RFQ's.

Q5) How does Council assess regional/office-location contribution for a Melbourne-based specialist that regularly works in adjoining Byron Shire and will use approved local subcontractors?

A5) Council will assess locality aspects from Local and Community criteria. It is suggested that any local sub-contractors are identified and location provided as part of Local and Community responses.

Q6) Can respondents submit the names of intended specialists and state that ABN, formal consent and evidence will be provided if shortlisted, or must each prospective subconsultant be formally committed at EOI close?

A6) It is suggested that a full list of possible sub-consultants be provided with their ABN.

Q7) For relevant-project value, will Council accept professional-service value as commercial-in-confidence (with a range or on-request disclosure), or is a numeric dollar figure mandatory?

A7) Respondents can provide a range of project value or provide no amount at all.

Q8) Does Council require the entire Quality, Environmental and WHS management system manuals or are approved policies, plan summaries and sample registers sufficient? Is ISO accreditation optional?

A8) Plan summaries are sufficient. Copies of accreditation would support any undertaking a respondent makes that they hold such accreditation.

Q9) For structural/temporary-works-only services under Roads and Traffic, must respondent hold a separate traffic-management/road safety accreditation, or is it acceptable for the traffic component to be separately subcontracted?

A9) Traffic compenents can be sub-contracted. Sun-contractors can be identified in the applicable requirement.

Q10) Are interstate engineers eligible for professional design roles subject to applicable NSW registration, and are there specific nominated disciplines/registration categories for this panel?

A10) Professional staff must hold valid registration in NSW for any services offered.

Q11) Are all seven categories intended to be accessible to small specialist firms, or will proposals be assessed against full-service requirements across each nominated category?

A11) Services for any sub-category can be offered.

Q12) Can Council provide its Statement of Business Ethics and confirm acceptable method of signing the Conflict of Interest declaration (electronic signature or signed PDF)?

A12) Councils Statement of Business ethics is available from Councils website via the link provided in the specifications. Electronic Signature of signed PDF are acceptable.

Q13) Will Council provide any standard panel deed, rate escalation provisions and interstate travel/disbursement policy before shortlisted respondents accept appointment?

A13) Council will issue an invited RFQ to applicable consultants from the shortlist which will include the scope/brief for works required on a case by case basis. The RFQ will specify the contract instrument and request fully itemised pricing.

Q14) Does Council intend to request specific local availability or maximum response times for emergency assessment call-outs, and may providers nominate advance mobilisation/lead times?

A14) Council will not specify or require any defined response times.

title: Queensland Government - Preferred Supplier Panel for Grocery, Dairy and Beverages

Queensland Government is seeking applications from Suppliers who wish to register to be a Preferred Supplier for Grocery, Dairy and Beverage Products. As part of this Preferred Supplier Panel we are accepting supplier applications at any time. The Preferred Supplier Panel categories include:

Grocery Products Dry Goods

Biscuits; baking mixes and supplies; flour and milled products; soups; stocks; powders; packaged desserts; savoury snacks; confectionary; nuts; grains; legumes; jelly; spreads; jams; preserves; sugar; sweetener; dry pasta; rice; noodles; cereals; oats; porridge; pulses; seasoning; dried herbs; spices; sauces; dressing; canned goods; vinegar; condiments; dried fruit; dried vegetables; fruit cups pureed fruit.

Frozen Goods

Meat; poultry; fish and seafood; vegetables; fruit; pies; pastries; cakes; generic prepared frozen meals; muffins; desserts, ice cream and convenience foods.

title: Top Dressing Blackwater/Bluff Sporting Fields
description:
Central Highlands Regional Council is seeking quotations from suitably qualified contractors to undertake sports field renovation works at nominated sporting fields within Blackwater and Bluff.

The works are intended to improve turf health, alleviate soil compaction, enhance drainage, improve playing surface quality, and support the long-term sustainability and safe use of community sporting facilities.

The successful contractor shall provide all labour, plant, equipment, materials and supervision necessary to undertake the following:

•	Solid Tine Aeration of nominated sporting fields using suitable sports turf equipment. (Only Blackwater Junior Rugby League Field)

•	Hollow Tine Aeration (Coring) to relieve soil compaction and improve root zone performance. (All fields except Junior League Field)

•	Collection, processing and management of extracted cores where required.

•	Apply Lime to Rugby Union Field Only @ 750kg/Ha. Water in from Irrigation

•	Supply and application of approved top dressing material.

•	Mechanical spreading and incorporation of top dressing to achieve a uniform surface finish of at least 30mm

•	Drag matting, brushing or similar finishing techniques to ensure even distribution of material.

•	Protection of existing turf, irrigation systems, drainage infrastructure and surrounding assets.

•	Removal and lawful disposal of waste materials generated during the works.

•	Site clean-up and reinstatement upon completion.

The Contractor is responsible for undertaking works in accordance with industry best practice, relevant workplace health and safety legislation, and manufacturer recommendations for all equipment used.

Works must be completed in a manner that minimises disruption to sporting clubs and facility users while maintaining safe access to surrounding areas. Any damage caused to Council assets during the works shall be rectified by the Contractor at no cost to Council.

Upon completion, the Contractor shall provide confirmation of:

•	Areas treated.

•	Aeration and coring methodology utilised.

•	Quantity and specification of top dressing material applied.

•	Any defects, irrigation faults or field condition issues identified during the works.

The completed surface must provide an even, safe and high-quality playing area suitable for community and competitive sporting use.

The Central Highlands region is in Central Queensland, Australia. The region encompasses an area of around 60 000 square kilometres, making it just short of the size of Tasmania.

Our region is rich in minerals and agriculture, thriving on irrigation sourced from water storage on the Nogoa and Comet rivers. We claim the largest sapphire-producing fields in the Southern Hemisphere.

Major freight routes through the region include the north-south link between Charters Towers and northern New South Wales—identified as the inland transport alternative between Cairns and Melbourne.

title: Long-Term Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country
description:
Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country (Long-Term) - WS5659204351

The Coordinator of Energy has determined, under clause 3.11A.4 of the Electricity System Market (ESM) Rules, to trigger a Non-Co-optimised Essential System Services (NCESS) procurement process by Western Power for Reliability and System Strength Services for the North Country.

The proposed services aim to address reliability and system strength concerns during planned or unplanned outage events affecting one or more 132 kV transmission lines supplying the North Country.

Western Power invites NCESS Submissions from prospective NCESS providers to deliver Reliability Services and/or System Strength Services located in the North Country. The North Country is defined as the area supplied by the Rangeway, Geraldton and Chapman substations.

This tender relates to the Long-Term contract term option (10-25 year terms). Proponents may offer a solution that fully or partially meets the requirements for either service (or both).

Activation requirements, performance measures, preferred connection locations and other technical requirements are set out in the Final NCESS Service Specification.

Queries may be submitted by email to emerging.technology.portfolio@westernpower.com.au or via the Q&A function in the VendorPanel portal.

Please submit NCESS Submissions via VendorPanel no later than 5:00pm (AWST) on 1 February 2027.

Interested NCESS providers should register with VendorPanel to be informed of whether any supporting documentation such as clarifications to questions may be published.

publicQuestions.answer:
Dear Respondents,

Please find response belowL

1. Which roles are in Category 2? Can Council supply a Job Dictionary for one of them?

Council is seeking information from the market proposing possible approaches to fitness for work assessments for roles. Vendors are encouraged to provide proposals that detail an approach for how Council could conduct suitable assessments for roles at different levels of the organisation. Council has not yet determined the ongoing requirement for this category, seeking to understand how the market foresees that such an undertaking could occur for a workforce of its diverse nature and varying levels of risk.

2. Roughly how many assessments a year?

Council engaged approximately 600 new starter employees in the past 12 months.

3. Should our results be recorded on the Suitable Duty Register, or in a separate report that maps to it?

The Suitable Duty Register is utilised in our Workers Compensation Return to Work program – it is not relevant to this engagement, albeit that it is included in the Job Dictionary template. The results of your assessments should be provided on your own report template, covering suitability for relevant aspects of the role.

4. Can a psychologist sign the register, given it asks for a "Doctor / Specialist"?

Yes, a suitably qualified psychologist could provide the report on the provider’s template as per the clarification in question 3 above.

5. Is telehealth acceptable for any or all of the assessment?

Providers are encouraged to outline their assessment methodology and suitable methods of interaction with our people based on ensuring that a reliable and replicable methodology can be utilised to ensure consistency in decision making.

6. Is Council looking for reports in prose and are there any pre-determine templates (acknowledging risk ratings matrix)?

Council is seeking a standardised template/s to be provided by the Provider, ensuring that there is a consistent application of Council’s risk matrix and that recommendations are made in light of Council’s terminology to assist review and decision-making. Council reserves the right to seek further clarification or additional information from the provider on individual assessments where required.

publicQuestions.answer:
1.	Programme modules and resources

The Specification refers to the delivery of mental health promotion modules for Years 7–10. Can Council confirm whether completed modules, session plans, facilitator guides, presentations and participant resources will be provided to the successful contractor, or whether development of these resources forms part of the contractor's scope?

Development of the programme modules and all associated resources forms part of the contractor's scope. Council will not provide existing programme content or curriculum resources for delivery. The successful provider may choose to source external facilitators that are content experts to support delivery of modules.

2.	Programme development

If the successful contractor is expected to develop or significantly adapt the educational content, can Council confirm the expected number and duration of modules, required deliverables and Council's review/approval process?

The Summary Program on a Page outlines potential program themes and content areas identified through co-design with young people, schools and other stakeholders.

Council proposes delivery of up to six (6) 60-minute topic-specific sessions throughout the school year. Tenderers should note the minimum delivery requirements outlined in the RFQ, being three (3) sessions per participating school in Year 1 and six (6) sessions per participating school in Year 2. If local needs are different to Council's proposed approach, there is flexibility in how the program objectives can be met i.e. a school may wish to have three two-hour sessions across the school year. The successful contractor will be expected to work collaboratively with young people and participating schools during the establishment phase to ensure the final program design, content and delivery approach are appropriate to local needs.

Should program content require modification during the contract period, any proposed changes should be discussed as part of scheduled contract meetings with council.

3.	School delivery volumes

Should tenderers base pricing on the stated minimum delivery requirements of three sessions per participating school in Year 1 and six sessions per participating school in Year 2, or should additional delivery volumes be allowed for? The specification sets minimum participation requirements but indicates final performance targets will be agreed prior to contract execution.

Tenderers should base pricing on the minimum delivery requirements outlined in the RFQ, being three (3) sessions per participating school in Year 1 and six (6) sessions per participating school in Year 2.

Council welcomes proposals that demonstrate the potential to deliver additional activities or outcomes within the available budget; however, pricing should clearly identify any assumptions regarding delivery volumes.

The total project budget is $296,000 (exclusive of GST), comprising $90,000 from January to June 2027, $148,000 from July 2027 to June 2028 and $58,000 from July 2028 to December 2028.

4.	School engagement

Have any secondary schools already indicated interest in participating, and what role will Council play in introducing the successful contractor and supporting engagement with schools?

Local secondary schools have been involved in the co-design of the program through a Reference Group established in early 2026. The successful contractor will be provided with opportunities to engage with the Reference Group and relevant school contacts as part of the establishment phase.

Council can confirm that local schools have expressed interest in participating in the program. Council will support initial introductions and relationship-building; however, ongoing engagement and partnership development with participating schools will be the responsibility of the successful contractor.

5. Life Skills & Resilience Expo

Can Council confirm the anticipated scale and requirements of each annual Life Skills & Resilience Expo, including expected attendance, duration, venue, AV, catering and external presenter/exhibitor requirements, and clarify which costs are expected to be met from the contract price?

All costs associated with planning, coordinating and delivering the Life Skills & Resilience Expo should be included within the proposed contract budget.

The Expo is intended to be available to all secondary school students within the municipality, as well as young people who are not currently engaged in a school setting.

The Summary Program on a Page outlines potential content and outcomes identified through the co-design process. The successful contractor will be expected to engage with young people and schools to determine detailed content, format and delivery requirements.

Council has not prescribed attendance numbers, venue requirements, catering, audio-visual requirements or exhibitor arrangements. Tenderers should propose an approach that can be delivered within the available budget and aligns with the objectives of the program and local needs.

6. Adult education

Can Council confirm the anticipated number, duration and participant numbers for education sessions for parents, carers, teachers and other adults, and whether Council has identified or developed content for this component?

The scope and format of the adult education component has not been prescribed by Council and should be proposed by the contractor as part of its response.

As outlined in the Summary Program on a Page, this component should support parents, carers and other trusted adults to strengthen connection with young people, manage family conflict and support the development of young people's emotional intelligence, resilience and wellbeing.

Stakeholders identified programs such as Tuning in to Kids as examples of approaches that may be considered; however, Council is open to alternative evidence-informed approaches that meet the objectives of the program.

7. Evaluation

Will Council provide an existing evaluation framework, baseline data and/or evaluation tools, or is the successful contractor expected to design the evaluation methodology and instruments?

As outlined in the program deliverables, the contractor will only be required to collect insights and feedback from young people, schools and community members to help demonstrate how the Program contributes to improving participants' knowledge, attitudes, confidence, skills and intended behaviours relating to mental health and wellbeing. This may include pre and post module surveys.

Council may elect to engage an independent external evaluator at the conclusion of the two-year pilot period to assess the overall impact and effectiveness of the Program. Data and feedback collected by the successful contractor throughout program delivery will be used to inform this evaluation.

8. Contract value and payment

Can Council confirm whether the stated $296,000 programme budget is exclusive of GST, and clarify the invoicing/payment milestones within the $90,000, $148,000 and $58,000 allocations? The contract provides for invoicing/payment arrangements rather than stating that the full funding is paid upfront.

The stated project budget of $296,000 is exclusive of GST.

The budget allocations of $90,000, $148,000 and $58,000 reflect Council's annual funding availability and budgeting requirements.

9. Intellectual property

Can Council clarify how clause 12.1 will apply where the successful contractor uses pre-existing educational content, tools, templates, methodologies or other intellectual property when developing or adapting resources for the programme?

Clause 12.1 applies to Intellectual Property Rights created by the successful contractor arising from or in connection with the delivery of the Services under this Contract.

Council does not intend clause 12.1 to transfer ownership of a contractor's pre-existing intellectual property, including existing educational content, tools, templates, methodologies or other materials developed independently of this Contract.

Where pre-existing intellectual property is incorporated into, adapted for, or required to use a deliverable developed under the Contract, the contractor will retain ownership of that pre-existing intellectual property. The contractor must, however, ensure that Council has sufficient rights to use the final deliverables for the purposes of the Youth Mental Health Promotion Program permanently.

Intellectual property created specifically in performing the Services under this Contract will vest in Council in accordance with clause 12.1.

title: Sports & Recreation Plan
description:
PREPARATION OF MCKINLAY SHIRE SPORT AND RECREATION PLAN

McKinlay Shire Council invites your firm to submit a written quotation for the provision of specialised consultancy services to develop a comprehensive, forward-looking Sport and Recreation Plan.

1. Project Overview & Background

Council is committed to fostering active, healthy, and connected communities across our region. To ensure our sport, active recreation, and community infrastructure effectively meet current and future needs, Council is seeking an experienced consultancy firm to undertake a complete review and redevelopment of our strategic framework for sport and recreation.

To assist in understanding our contextual foundation and strategic alignment, Council will provide successful respondents/tenderers with copies of:

•	McKinlay Shire Council 2010 Sport and Recreation Plan

•	McKinlay Shire Council Community Strategic Plan 2019-2026

•	McKinlay Shire Council Corporate Plan 2025-2030

2. Scope of Services

The successful consultant will be required to deliver an end-to-end plan, incorporating the following core stages and tasks:

1.	In-Region Site Inspection & Facility Assessment

o	Conduct an on-site visit to the region to inspect existing sport, recreation, and community facilities (including sports grounds, arenas, aquatic centre, indoor spaces, tennis courts, gym, parks, and trails).

o	Assess facility condition, functionality, spatial coverage, maintenance/lifecycle status, and opportunities for upgrading or multi-use optimisation.

2.	Strategic Direction & Alignment

o	Review relevant local, regional, and state sport and recreation policies, funding guidelines, and demographic trends.

o	Align proposed strategy directly with Council’s overarching Strategic Plan and regional priorities.

3.	Community & Stakeholder Engagement

o	Design and execute a robust community consultation strategy targeting local residents, sporting clubs, community groups, schools, Health Service and key regional stakeholders.

o	Conduct online and physical surveys, public workshops/drop-in sessions, and targeted interviews with key sporting association representatives and community members.

o	Engage regularly with appropriate Council Staff and Elected Members to identify current and future needs for Sport and Recreation across the Shire

4.	Executive Presentations & Governance Engagement

o	Attend an initial on-site meeting to present preliminary findings, scope alignment, and key emerging themes to Council's Senior Executive Leadership Team and Elected Members.

o	Attend an on-site meeting upon completion to present the final draft plan and executive briefing prior to formal Council adoption.

publicQuestions.question:
Good Morning, just a few questions:

1.	Scope: Does the tender consider passive recreation or is the focus on active and sport?

2.	Tourism: will this be a consideration within the plan?

3.	Auditing and Mapping: is open space mapping a requirement of the brief and if so is this just the main townships?

4.	Play: Are playspaces to be considered and if so how many do you currently have?

5.	Facility assessment: What level of assessment is required? Should this be a strategic visual assessment, or is Council expecting detailed condition audits?

6.	Consultation: What consultation coverage does Council expect across townships? Will Council assist with contact, promotion, venues and meeting arrangements?

7.	Schedule: What commencement date, draft review period and final delivery date does Council anticipate? Is there a target date for Council adoption?

8.	Future needs: Are there particular population, workforce or industry changes Council wants the plan to consider, such as mining and critical minerals projects, tourism etc?

10.	Budget and pricing: Has Council set a budget range or maximum contract value?

thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
Good morning, Mark

Scope: The Sport and Recreation Plan aims to evaluate our existing facilities and support local sporting clubs, providing actionable recommendations to enhance and advance sport and recreation opportunities across the Shire.

Tourism: Yes, tourism opportunities and visitor usage must be integrated into the plan.

Auditing and Mapping: Open space spatial mapping is a core component. Mapping will establish the baseline spatial data required for Council’s future asset management, infrastructure planning, and grant applications. Coverage includes Julia Creek, McKinlay, Nelia, Kynuna, Combo Waterhole, and surrounding rural areas.

Playspaces & Assets: Playspaces are included. Key assets to cover include:

McKinlay: Township playspace and tennis courts.

Julia Creek: Eastern approach playspace (Flinders Highway), main town center playspace, caravan park precinct (putt-putt golf, traffic training area, tennis & basketball courts, outdoor gym, public pool & slide, Kev Bannon Oval, bike path, and skate park).

Outlying Locations: Key recreational/visitor nodes including Combo Waterhole and Kynuna facilities.

Facility Assessment: A strategic visual and functional condition assessment (e.g., identifying aging equipment, safety compliance, and maintenance needs).

Consultation: Council requires a hybrid engagement model, including a community workshop in Julia Creek and an online/paper survey for remote and outlying residents. Council will host public sessions and promote consultation via our weekly newsletter, Facebook, and local flyers.

Schedule: Council has not set fixed milestone dates and expects the successful tenderer to propose a realistic project schedule and timeframe.

Future Drivers & Growth: Planning must address population changes linked to local mining growth while heavily prioritizing community liveability to attract and retain long-term residents. Enhancing tourism infrastructure remains a high priority to support regional economic development and local employment.

Budget & Pricing: A formal budget has not yet been resolved by Council. Tenderers should submit a detailed cost breakdown based on their proposed methodology.

publicQuestions.question:
In Appendix 1 – Functional and Technical Specification, clause 3.1.2.2 and Section 3.2.3 call for single logical-unit and stacking options, while Tables 7 and 8 (clauses 2.4.7.1–2.4.7.2) specify stacked Layer-three switches at MAN and WAN Class 2B sites. Section 3.2.3 also requires SC switches to operate SR-MPLS with Flexible Algorithm and TI-LFA. Can CITEC confirm whether these routing features and stacking must operate together on the same switches, or whether independent redundant devices are acceptable? If both cannot be supported together, which requirement takes priority?

Question Regarding: PART C Capability Response

PSNMC has provided data in the column "Customer Defined Criticality"; That entry matches one of the six columns "Offerors Select" for the various site criticality classes. Does the responder need to complete all 6 columns per site, or only the column that matches the column "Customer Defined Criticality"?
publicQuestions.answer:
In Appendix 1 – Functional and Technical Specification, clause 3.1.2.2 and Section 3.2.3 call for single logical-unit and stacking options, while Tables 7 and 8 (clauses 2.4.7.1–2.4.7.2) specify stacked Layer-three switches at MAN and WAN Class 2B sites. Section 3.2.3 also requires SC switches to operate SR-MPLS with Flexible Algorithm and TI-LFA. Can CITEC confirm whether these routing features and stacking must operate together on the same switches, or whether independent redundant devices are acceptable? If both cannot be supported together, which requirement takes priority?

CITEC does not require these routing capabilities and stacking functionality to operate together on the same physical switch platform, provided that:

The proposed solution delivers the required routing functionality, resilience, availability, and operational outcomes.

The architecture provides equivalent or better levels of redundancy and failover capability.

Accordingly, independent redundant devices are acceptable where they meet the functional and operational intent of the specification.

Where a bidder's proposed platform cannot support both stacking and the specified routing capabilities simultaneously, bidders should clearly identify this within their response and describe the alternative architecture proposed.

Question Regarding: PART C Capability Response

PSNMC has provided data in the column "Customer Defined Criticality"; That entry matches one of the six columns "Offerors Select" for the various site criticality classes. Does the responder need to complete all 6 columns per site, or only the column that matches the column "Customer Defined Criticality"?

Please complete only the column that matches the 'Customer Defined Criticality'.

Please confirm the scope split. Please also confirm that any flange mounted flow transmitters would be installed in piping by the mechanical contractor and wired by the E&I contractor.

2. Are cables listed in the cable schedule as "special" to be assumed as pre-terminated flex rubber cables connected to submersible pumps and therefore free issued?

4. Are native CAD files for drawings presented in tender document package going to be issued to the successful bidder?

6. Is design/installation of site lighting system required?

publicQuestions.answer:
1. All instruments and associated mounting brackets and supports will be installed under the Civil and Mechanical Package. This includes the mechanical installation of flange-mounted flow transmitters within the pipework.

The Electrical and Instrumentation (E&I) contractor is responsible for cabling, termination and electrical connection of all instruments and equipment from the relevant field location, junction box or local control station back to the switchboard.

Cables identified as “special” are to be assessed according to the equipment they serve, as follows:

2. Cables identified as “special” are to be assessed according to the equipment they serve, as follows:

Pond mixers: The E&I contractor shall supply and install the cables from the local control station to the terminal box on each mixer. These cables shall be suitable for floating service over the ponds and secured to the mooring cable between the mixer and its mooring anchor. These cables will not be free-issued. Tenderers shall identify the cables and associated equipment included in their offer and clearly state any assumptions.

Submersible pumps: The special cables associated with the submersible pumps will be included in the pump supply and may therefore be excluded from the E&I contractor’s cable supply allowance.

3. Council is unable to confirm the number of cores at this stage, as the relevant vendor information has not yet been provided. Tenderers shall make suitable allowances and clearly identify their assumptions regarding cable core numbers in their tender submissions, to enable subsequent clarification where required.

4. Yes. Native CAD files for the drawings included in the tender documentation will be supplied to the successful tenderer.

5. Building power and earthing design are included in the E&I contractor’s scope. Building lighting is already documented in the drawing set and shall be allowed for accordingly. No additional site lighting beyond that shown on the drawings is currently anticipated.

6. No additional site lighting system is required at this stage. The E&I contractor shall allow for the lighting nominated on the tender drawings.

7. Temporary power to maintain operation of the existing facility during installation is not currently expected to be required.

For construction activities, site power will be available from the 100 kVA transformer through the main switchboard. The E&I contractor shall provide any distribution board and temporary distribution arrangements required to undertake its own scope of works. Other contractors are responsible for making provision for their respective construction power requirements.

General

Tenderers shall clearly state any assumptions regarding power availability, connection arrangements and temporary power requirements in their tender submissions.

title: Remove and Replace Roof Structures, Opal Street WTP Filters
description:
Central Highlands Regional Council operates the Opal Street Water Treatment Plant (WTP) located in Emerald, Queensland. The WTP incorporates four rapid gravity sand filters which form a critical component of the potable water treatment process.

Each filter is currently protected by an individual structural steel roof structure. Over time, these roof structures have deteriorated and are approaching the end of their serviceable life. In addition to their deteriorated condition, the existing roof structures do not adequately facilitate the operational requirements associated with periodic filter media replacement.

During future filter media replacement campaigns, one-tonne bulk sandbags are required to be lowered into the filter compartments via crane. The existing roof structures do not provide suitable openings through which these bags can be safely lowered into the filters. This creates operational difficulties and increases risk during maintenance activities.

Central Highlands Regional Council is seeking responses from suitably qualified and experienced contractors to undertake the design, removal, disposal, supply and construction of replacement roof structures over the four rapid gravity filters.

The replacement roof structures must incorporate suitable access openings that facilitate the future lowering of one-tonne bulk bags of filter media into each filter compartment by others under a separate contract.

The Works are to be delivered under a Design and Construct Contract.

The Contractor must provide all labour, design services, engineering services, supervision, plant, equipment, materials, transport, certifications and incidentals required to complete the Works.

The Works include, but are not limited to:

• Site inspection and verification of existing conditions.

• Detailed design of replacement roof structures for four rapid gravity sand filters.

• Structural design certification by a Registered Professional Engineer of Queensland (RPEQ).

• Preparation and submission of design documentation and drawings.

• Attendance at, facilitation of and incorporation of feedback from an 80% design review workshop with Central Highlands Regional Council Water Utilities personnel. The Contractor must present theproposed design, demonstrate how operational requirements have been addressed, and provide draft design documentation for review prior to finalisation of the design.

• Removal and lawful disposal of existing roof structures. This includes the temporary covering of the sand filter opening to avoid any contaminants entering the filter media.

• Supply and installation of new roof structures.

• Provision of access openings to facilitate future filter media replacement activities.

• Supply and installation of all structural steelwork, roofing, flashings, lighting, stormwater runoff piping to prevent filter contamination, fixings and protective coatings.

• Final inspection and commissioning.

• Provision of as-constructed drawings and documentation.

• Handover of the completed Works.

The Contractor must be responsible for delivering a complete and fit-for-purpose solution.

Prior to commencing work on site, the Contractor must prepare, submit, revise and implement project-specific management plans suitable for the Works, including safety/WHS, environmental, quality, demolition, construction methodology/site management and traffic/pedestrian/access management plans, as applicable.

The replacement of filter media is specifically excluded from this Contract and will be undertaken by others under a separate contract.

Where the Opal St WTP Filter Media Replacement technical specification prepared by AECOM is provided with this RFT, only Sections 3.0 Materials and Construction, 4.0 Design and Documentation and 5.0 Roof Structure Removal and Reinstatement apply to this Contract, and only to the extent relevant to the design, removal, disposal, supply and construction of replacement roof structures. All other sections of that document are provided for information only unless expressly referenced in this Specification. In the event of inconsistency, this Specification takes precedence.

The Contractor must supply all labour, supervision, engineering services, design services, plant, equipment, materials, transport, temporary works and incidentals necessary to complete the Works.

The Works must be undertaken at the Opal Street Water Treatment Plant, Opal Street, Emerald, Queensland.

The Contract will commence within 7 days after the Award Letter and Contractual Arrangement are provided to and signed by the successful Contractor. Central Highlands Regional Council anticipates the contract end date to be as per the approved contract schedule.

Good day,

Thanks for the Site visit.

Can you clearly define the Battery limits on the Existing concrete structure.

The RFT says the contractor’s design must include verification of the existing support structures, foundations, dimensions, levels, interfaces and affected services.

This as stated is no small task and I am unsure of the intent. Due to the level of movement of the structure that was noted and commented on by CHRC rep it is evident that the current foundations have had issues. Further to this The AECOM specification is relevant here because it actually contains a dedicated “Concrete Rehabilitation” section, covering concrete breakout/removal, exposed reinforcement treatment, substrate preparation, repair materials, reinstatement, finishing, curing, inspection and testing. So I need to understand a clear battery limit.

The design requirements also explicitly say the new roof design must “include lighting and rainwater disposal.”

Can you please provide the Design or Design intent for both of these items. Where is the power coming from? Has the engineering been completed? What lights do you require and where? How many of them? Where is the rain water to go? What are the tie in points? Sorry but the CHRC Rep was not aware of any of the details.

The CHRC Rep was of the understanding that these roof structures were to fully enclose the WTP filters down and sealed onto the concrete, completely sealed from wind and rain water, also vermin proff. Please confirm this is the intent that a fully sealed area is required not just replacement roof structures.

Can you confirm the expected shutdown/staging arrangement? Can only one complete filter pair/two cells be taken offline at a time, and must each filter be completely returned to service before the next roof is removed?

What is the maximum allowable outage for each filter? Is there a preferred low-demand period or particular months when Council wants construction undertaken?

Are there existing structural drawings for all four filter concrete structures? We understand the filters were built at different times and may not be identical.

Does Council have a preferred new roof arrangement? Skillion, gable, similar to existing, or is the geometry entirely contractor-designed?

What corrosion protection system does Council expect for the structural steel? Is hot-dip galvanising acceptable/preferred, or is a duplex/coating system required? The new design has a minimum 25-year service-life requirement.

Please clarify exactly how Council expects the two access openings per filter to operate. Must operators be able to physically open them without mechanical lifting equipment, or is crane removal of a roof cassette acceptable?

Is the specified minimum 2 m × 2 m clear opening required for each individual filter cell without exception?

How does Council envisage the one-tonne bulk bags being lowered through the roof? What crane/telehandler will normally be used, and from which side of each filter?

If removable roof sections are acceptable, does Council require permanent certified lifting points and a documented lifting procedure?

What permanent working-at-heights system is expected? Static line, fall-arrest anchors, ladder attachment points, roof access walkway, or simply engineered attachment provisions?

What temporary protection is required over the open filters during demolition and construction? Does Council require a rigid engineered cover, sealed membrane system, or another defined standard?

Can a reusable temporary filter cover be moved progressively from Filter 1 to Filter 4, or does Council require multiple covers to be available simultaneously?

Are there contamination-control requirements beyond physically covering the filter? For example restrictions on grinding, hot work, galvanised material handling, drilling, dust generation or chemicals near an operating filter.

Can we perform hot works above/adjacent to the filters once an approved temporary cover is fitted? Or does Council expect essentially all cutting/welding to be completed off site?

Where can cranes be positioned for each of the four filters? We need to establish available radius and likely crane capacity.

Are there known underground services beneath the proposed crane/outrigger locations? Can Council supply service plans?

Does Council have information on pavement/ground bearing capacity for crane outriggers? If not, what verification will be required?

Who performs plant isolations — Council operators or AMM? What notice period is required?

Is condensation underneath the roof currently an issue? Does Council expect insulation or anti-condensation roof backing?

Townsville City Council (Landowner/Trustee) invites submissions from community and/or sporting organisations, incorporated associations, charities and not-for-profit entities seeking to lease and operate the community facility (building only) located 95-111 Queens Road, Hermit Park QLD 4812.

The premises are situated on land dedicated for Park and Recreation purposes and may only be used for activities that are consistent with the Reserve purpose and the approved use outlined in the Trustee Lease.

Council intends to offer a five (5) year lease term to the successful applicant at a nominal (peppercorn) rent of $1.00 per annum (excluding GST), if demanded. The peppercorn rent recognises the not-for-profit community purpose of the lease and is offered on the basis that the lessee delivers ongoing community benefit and meets all outgoings and obligations under the lease. The lease will provide an opportunity for an organisation to occupy and manage the facility for the purpose of delivering club, community and charitable activities that contribute to the social, recreational and community wellbeing of the local area.

title: West Moreton Bridge Renewal Stage 2
description:
Queensland Rail is seeking to engage a Principal Contractor to deliver the West Moreton Bridge Renewal Stage 2 Project under a Design & Construct (D&C) delivery model. The project involves the replacement of four existing timber rail bridges at two locations on the Rosewood to Toowoomba section of the West Moreton System, at chainages 56.600 km and 59.230 km.

The works will broadly include the design and construction of new concrete ballast deck bridges, demolition of the existing structures, associated track, formation, drainage and access works, and testing, certification and handover. The works will be delivered within a live operational rail environment and will require construction planning and staging to accommodate rail possession and access constraints

vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription:
The Gwydir Shire is in the centre of the ‘Fossickers Way’, a route which offers the traveller a relaxing alternative to the New England or Newell Highways. The Shire encompasses a diverse landscape that is both picturesque and productive and is approximately 560 km north of Sydney, 160 km north of Tamworth along the Fossickers Way and 85 km north-west of Inverell. The shire is 9,122 square kilometres in size and is situated north of Tamworth Regional Council and continues almost to the Queensland border.

The southern boundary of the shire is the Nandewar Range where the Gwydir and Namoi Valleys meet. The Horton Valley and Cobbadah District are home to some Australia’s most highly regarded beef cattle studs. These enterprising farmers use the latest artificial breeding and agronomic technology to produce beef of exceptional quality. Meat Sheep and merinos that grow high quality wool are also grazed in this area.

The Gwydir River enters the Gwydir Shire where it spills from the Copeton Dam and meanders in a westerly direction through the towns of Bingara and Gravesend. The Gwydir valley is well know for irrigated and dry land cropping as well as livestock production. In addition to the traditional crops of wheat, barley, oats and sorghum, there are olive groves, pecan nut plantations and freshwater fish farms in the Gravesend district.

Heading northwest from the timbered surrounds of the town of Warialda and the close-knit community of Coolatai, the countryside opens into an undulating vista of basalt farmland. This part of the Shire which include the villages of Crooble, Croppa Creek and North Star, is known as the ‘Golden Triangle’. Farmers using advanced farming techniques, such as minimum tillage and satellite guidance systems, produce a variety of high yielding crops such as wheat, barley sorghum, maize, chick peas, canola and cotton to name just a few. This area also has several cattle feed lots which supply grain fed beef to the Australian domestic market and export markets throughout the world.

Both Warialda and Bingara have Hospitals, Aged Care Hostels, Medical Centres, Caravan Parks, Swimming Pools, Pre-schools, Libraries, Tourist Information Centres, and a Mobile Pre-school based at North Star. Warialda is the centre for the Council’s Technical Services functions. Bingara is the centre for the Administrative functions. The two centres are being linked through the use of sophisticated communications equipment to ensure that the amalgamations primary objective is achieved which is to save the existing employment numbers within each of the main urban centres of Warialda and Bingara.
