vendorPanelDetails.background:
The consultancy forms part of Council’s integrated FOGO Program, comprising the processing facility, collection service transition, and education and behaviour change projects. The successful Consultant will report to Council’s FOGO Program Manager and coordinate with Waste Services, Communications and Engagement teams, and relevant contractors through Council-approved arrangements.

The MidCoast includes towns, villages and dispersed rural communities with different waste service arrangements. Current arrangements include standard three-bin services, rural two-bin services and properties without a green bin. These arrangements do not, by themselves, establish future FOGO eligibility. Campaign content must use Council-confirmed service information so residents receive instructions applicable to their property and implementation stage.

The campaign must:

- Align with Council’s Education and Behaviour Change Strategy, Plan Framework and branding requirements.

- Address audience needs identified through the supplied evidence and approved research, including accessibility, literacy, digital access and rural communication needs.

- Integrate Council-owned channels with appropriate television, social media, digital, print, newspaper, billboard and other physical media.

- Include reusable materials for community stalls, displays and education activities.

- Provide accessible final outputs and editable source files, templates, records and campaign assets that Council can maintain and adapt.

Facility readiness controls service commencement. Tenderers must demonstrate how they will sequence early research and reusable work, manage approval gates, and reprogram or pause activities while minimising avoidable expenditure. The response schedules include common 3-, 6- and 12-month delay scenarios for evaluation purposes; these are not forecast delays or guaranteed additional work.

Council’s tender documents define the detailed requirements, acceptance criteria, pricing arrangements and conditions of contract.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes:
Council seeks a practical, evidence-based campaign that builds community understanding and supports correct participation in the FOGO service before, during and after its introduction.

Desired outcomes include:

- Clear, consistent and service-specific information that helps residents understand what changes, when it changes and how to use their service correctly.

- Research-informed messages and activities that address behavioural barriers and motivators.

- Accessible engagement that reaches relevant audiences across the MidCoast.

- Reliable delivery of approved campaign assets, media and community activities.

- Transparent reporting on outputs, reach, engagement and behavioural outcomes, distinguishing the Consultant’s contribution from factors controlled by service design, facility performance or other parties.

- A complete handover that enables Council or another supplier to maintain and adapt the campaign.

Council will assess relevant experience, behaviour change capability, methodology, delivery capacity, program flexibility, demonstrated outcomes and value for money. Tenderers may identify optional enhancements separately, with their benefits and costs clearly stated.

The contract requires defined deliverables, documented approvals, regular program and risk reporting, and written acceptance against agreed criteria. Correction of poor work, errors, omissions or non-compliance is the Consultant’s responsibility and does not consume an included review round.

Publication, launch activities and non-refundable commitments require the applicable written Council approvals. Changes to scope, fees or delivery dates must follow the contract’s authorisation processes. Critical milestones and delay damages apply as specified in Part B.

The Consultant must also meet the contract’s professional standards, insurance, privacy, security, intellectual property, accessibility, records, safety and handover requirements. Council requires transparency about subcontractors, third-party costs, supplier benefits and proposed use of AI.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
The successful Tenderer shall:

- Be accredited by the National Association of Testing Authorities (NATA), or equivalent accreditation body under ISO/IEC 17025.

- Environmental monitoring of Wastewater, Waste & Resource to comply with the “Approved methods for the sampling and analysis of water pollutants in NSW” guideline issued by the Environment Protection Authority of NSW.

- PFAS monitoring of water supplies to align with the Australian Drinking Water Guidelines (ADWG) monitoring units

- PFAS monitoring of Wastewater, Waste & Resource to align with Environmental Protection Agency Landfill and Sewerage Treatment Plant PFAS Monitoring Chemical Control Order (CCO)

The Council requires the successful tenderer to demonstrate capacity to accept AHOC samples for emergency and unplanned environmental testing events outside of the routine scheduled monitoring program. Acceptance of these samples will require a acceptance response within 2- 24 hours of request. Such events may arise from, but are not limited to, sewage overflows, treatment plant bypasses, receiving waterway pollution incidents, community complaints regarding water quality, post-flood or extreme weather events, suspected contamination of a water supply or reticulation network, or environmental incidents. In these circumstances, the tenderer must be capable of mobilising sample collection and analytical resources within a timeframe agreed with Council, which may include after-hours, weekend, or public holiday response.

Emergency analytical results shall be communicated to Council electronically at within 12 days of samples being delivered to the laboratory, with a formal written report to follow within the timeframe specified by Council. Exceptions to this clause may apply when emergency testing requires immediate action with results delivered within 1 day of results being available. The tenderer shall maintain adequate surge capacity to manage emergency testing concurrently with existing scheduled workloads without compromising the quality or timeliness of routine analytical services. Pricing for emergency callout and priority analysis shall be clearly itemised as a separate schedule within the tender response.

Methods of conducting the tests must comply with the Table 1 of “Approved methods for the sampling and analysis of water pollutants in NSW”

Transport and delivery costs must be included in tendered rates.

BIODIESEL PRODUCTION CHEMICAL REQUIREMENTS

Hi Team,

My name is Sam and our team will be bidding for this under our brand Arkki. We run these classes directly in schools, childcares and with other local councils. We actually build specific programs similar to this and run them term by term inside schools. We are happy to work with your team to build a specific program for local schools inside of the Penrith LGA.

We are preparing our quotation and would appreciate clarification on the following points so we can submit a complete and accurately costed proposal.

1. Available budget and committed delivery volume

Is Council able to disclose an indicative budget range, excluding GST? Should the stated 80 delivery days be treated as a minimum committed purchase? If bookings are lower than anticipated, is there any minimum purchase commitment?

2. What the daily rate should cover

Does Council have a preference for four or five sessions per day, and a preferred session duration within the stated 40–60 minutes? Are most bookings expected to be full days at one school, or should we allow for a material number of standalone sessions or partial-day bookings?

3. Student numbers and school supervision

What typical and maximum student numbers should we allow for per session, and are combined classes anticipated? Will a school teacher remain present throughout each session to support supervision and behaviour management, with school support staff available where required?

4. School recruitment, handover and commencement

Will Council provide the successful supplier with an existing school contact list, previous participation or booking information, any provisional 2027 bookings and introductions to participating schools? What promotional support will Council provide, and when would this handover occur?

5. Cancellations, reduced bookings and unused days

What notice periods and payment arrangements apply when a school cancels, postpones or reduces a booking? If a booked day proceeds with fewer classes than planned, would the agreed day rate remain payable or would individual-session rates apply? Can unused term allocations move to a later term, and how would Council treat unfilled days where the supplier has completed the agreed school recruitment activities?

6. Lesson content, materials and approval

Should schools select a focused topic from an approved program menu, or is each session expected to cover a prescribed combination of topics? Are individual take-home projects, printed student materials or teacher follow-up resources required?

What approved local waste information and existing resources will Council supply? Would Council like to work with us in providing reusable materials that we would implement in our programs? If so - is there a cost to us for this?

7. Resource handover and ongoing use

For the learning resources supplied under the program, what must be handed over to Council, including any editable files? Does Council require the ability to deliver, adapt or distribute those resources independently or after the contract ends?

8. Payment for initial development and setup

If initial program development, resource preparation and educator training are separately itemised in the quotation, can those costs be invoiced when the agreed setup deliverables are accepted by Council? Alternatively, does Council require these costs to be recovered through the delivery rates?

Thank you for helping us clarify these points.
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Available budget and committed delivery volume

80 delivery days (20 per term) should be treated as a guide for the expected service. Council finds this schedule currently works well for contractors to secure school bookings but are willing to negotiate a higher or reduced schedule depending on the quoted cost and capacity of the successful supplier.

2. What the daily rate should cover

Council does not have a specific preference for these options and are happy with 4 or 5 sessions a day that run anywhere between 40-60 minutes. In our experience, most schools book a full day however smaller schools with less students may only require 2 sessions. On these days Council is happy for the schedule to be split between schools i.e. morning spent at one school, afternoon spent at another if possible.

3. Student numbers and school supervision

This varies from school to school depending on class sizes but usually the maximum is around 30 students (smaller schools may combine classes and run a session for the entire grade or stage, larger schools usually book for individual classes), Council are happy for the successful contractor to have these conversations with the schools during the booking process. In our experience, a teacher has always been present to supervise and support behaviour management.

4. School recruitment, handover and commencement

Council will be able to provide an existing school contact list, but outreach further to this will be the responsibility of the successful supplier. Council has a limited capacity to promote the service but does make mention at relevant events and meetings e.g. Penrith Hawkesbury Environment Educator Network. The successful supplier will be expected to begin seeking bookings for Term 1 2027 upon being awarded the contract. Council understands this is a busy time of year for schools and Term 1 bookings may be difficult to fully book.

5. Cancellations, reduced bookings and unused days

As mentioned in the RFQ the agreement with our current supplier is for 20 days per term (this is invoiced to Council at the end of the school term and paid accordingly) with bookings and cancelations managed between the schools and the supplier. Council is flexible with unforeseen changes in programming and would work with the successful applicant to manage these changes to ensure expected works are completed realistically. For example, in 2026 a primary school cancelled a week before their session and we worked with our contractor to offer these sessions to Council run childcare centres as a one off to fill the availability. Suppliers should make sure to include any cancelation fees or timeframes in their response to the RFQ and if they have any contingency plans in place. It is up to suppliers if they include just an individual session rate, just a day rate or both these rates in the schedule of rates. If providing a day rate, suppliers should clearly state how many sessions they include in a day rate. Unused term allocations can be moved to a later term e.g. if Council and the supplier agree on 20 days a term and the supplier only fills 18 days, Council are happy for 22 days to be booked the following term to make up the difference.

6. Lesson content, materials and approval

The successful supplier will offer a range of topics and lesson content should be focused on the categories provided in the RFQ. Schools generally select a single topic from a list provided by the supplier e.g. FOGO, litter, recycling, plastic free, etc. If the supplier is developing new content, Council is happy to review material to ensure it aligns with Council’s resource recovery objectives and Penrith specific waste services. Individual take-home projects and follow-up teaching resources are not required, with the focus being the on the day incursion. If the supplier wishes to supply these additional resources they should be included in additional items on the schedule of rates. Council is able to provide advice and digital copies of information on local waste information if required e.g. sorting guide. The supply and cost of any physical resources or materials used in the program are the responsibility of the supplier and should be included in the quoted amount.

7. Resource handover and ongoing use

Council reserves the right to check any resources supplied or handed out as part of the program for accuracy. Council does not require the ability to deliver, adapt or distribute these resources independently or after the contract ends.

8. Payment for initial development and setup

Program development, resource preparation and educator training can be itemised separately in the schedule of rates. Council is happy to discuss any set up costs with the successful supplier and come to an agreement to be invoiced for these items ahead of delivery.

publicQuestions.question:
Can we please clarify:

1) Is the successful supplier providing and tailoring for PCC its own educational program and resources, or is the supplier to deliver an existing program/content supplied by PCC?

2) If program development or adaptation for PCC is required, is there a separate budget for this work, and should respondents identify a one-off development fee in the Schedule of Rates, or incorporate these costs into the session/day rates?

3) If Council supplies the program, should quotations cover only promotion, scheduling, delivery and reporting, or are any content development or resource production services also required?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. The successful supplier is expected to provide and tailor their own education prgram and resources.

2. Program development, resource preparation and educator training can be itemised separately in the schedule of rates.

3. As above, the successful supplier will be expected to develop and deliver the program. Development and resource production should be itemised separately on the schedule of rates. Council is happy to discuss any set up costs with the successful supplier, help suggest and review materials and come to an agreement about being invoiced for these items ahead of delivery of the education sessions to schools.

publicQuestions.question:
Could Council please clarify whether the reference to 4–5 sessions/classes per day reflects a preference for delivery to individual classroom-sized groups, or is an indicative arrangement?

Alongside a conforming quotation, would Council welcome an optional delivery format as multi-year level/whole-school groupings across fewer sessions, provided the program remains age-appropriate, meets the educational objectives and offers comparable or greater student reach within the available budget?
publicQuestions.answer:
Council's preference is that the successful provider deliver 4-5 sessions per day to classroom sized groups (larger schools will generally book in 4-5 individual class sessions in a day e.g. book in 4-5 year 3 classes throughout the day, whereas smaller schools with lower class sizes, may combine classes and have sessions based on delivery to either a whole grade or stage e.g. a Kindergarten session, a years 1-2 session, a years 3-4 session and a years 5-6 session). Generally this format has worked well for schools and run smoothly for booking and delivery by the supplier.

Council is more than happy to receive optional delivery formats as listed in your question and consider alternative ways to deliver the school education program provided we also receive a conforming quotation as part of the supplier's response.

With reference to Clause 3.5 of the Draft Services Contract and Schedule 3 – Price Indices, could Council please confirm whether tenderers may propose a separate diesel fuel price adjustment mechanism based on a nominated base diesel price of $2.00 per litre (excluding GST), with adjustments linked to the Fuel – Brisbane Index (Index 10)?

Would this be considered a conforming tender, or would it need to be submitted as an alternative non-conforming tender alongside a conforming offer?
publicQuestions.answer:
Thank you for your enquiry.

The Contract Price review mechanism nominated in the Draft Services Contract for WRR/39/2027 is Index No. 1 of Schedule 3 – General goods and services (Brisbane All Groups CPI). Council has not nominated a separate diesel fuel price adjustment mechanism for the Contract.

Tenderers should therefore submit a conforming offer based on the requirements of the Tender Documents, including the Contract Price review mechanism contained in the Draft Services Contract.

If a tenderer wishes to propose a separate diesel fuel price adjustment mechanism, this may be submitted as an alternative non-conforming offer, provided that a conforming offer is also submitted. In accordance with the Tender Conditions, the alternative offer must clearly identify all instances of non-conformance.

The proposed departure should be clearly identified in Form 4 – Contract Compliance. Form 4 requires tenderers to identify the relevant clause or condition, indicate whether the offer is partially compliant or non-compliant, explain the reason for the departure and provide any other relevant information.

For a proposed diesel fuel price adjustment mechanism, sufficient information should be provided to allow Council to understand the proposal.

Submission of an alternative non-conforming offer does not constitute Council's acceptance of the proposed departure.

publicQuestions.question:
Clarification regarding eLearning and Instructional Design Services

We note that this opportunity has been advertised under the VendorPanel categories *Content Development & Instructional Design* and *eLearning Services & Solutions*.

Our organisation specialises in the design and development of customised digital learning solutions, including instructional design, interactive eLearning, online WHS and compliance training, and the conversion of existing training materials into digital formats.

While the Technical Specification identifies nine separable portions focused on training delivery, we would appreciate clarification on whether Council is also seeking suppliers for standalone instructional design, eLearning development or digital training content services under this Preferred Supplier Arrangement.

If these services are within scope, could Council please advise how suppliers should nominate and price them within the tender response schedules?
publicQuestions.answer:
Good morning,

Thank you for your enquiry.

While this Preferred Supplier Arrangement has been advertised under categories that may encompass content development, instructional design and eLearning services, the primary scope of this tender is the provision of the training services and separable portions described in the Technical Specification.

Council is not seeking to establish a Preferred Supplier Arrangement for standalone instructional design, eLearning development, digital content creation, online compliance training, or the conversion of existing training materials into digital formats under this procurement. Accordingly, suppliers are not required to nominate or submit pricing for these standalone services within the tender response schedules.

However, where eLearning, virtual delivery, digital learning resources, or other technology-enabled training methods support the delivery of a specified training service within a separable portion, Council welcomes these approaches as part of a supplier's proposed training solution. Tenderers are encouraged to outline any such capabilities in their response where they enhance accessibility, flexibility, learner engagement, or value for money.

Council does not currently have a dedicated arrangement for the provision of standalone instructional design or eLearning development services. Should such services be required in the future, Council would procure them in accordance with its standard procurement processes, seeking quotations from suitably qualified suppliers as required.

Tenderers should therefore focus their submissions and pricing on the training services identified within the Request for Tender documentation, while highlighting any relevant eLearning or digital delivery capabilities that form part of their proposed service offering.

Kind Regards,

LSC Procurement Team

publicQuestions.question:
Good morning,

We are currently completing the tender documentation and would appreciate clarification regarding Tender Schedule 5 – Insurance Details, specifically the requirements for Motor Vehicle Registration and Compulsory Third-Party (CTP) Insurance.

As vehicle registration and CTP insurance in Queensland are managed electronically through the Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR), physical registration certificates are no longer routinely issued.

Could you please confirm what form of evidence Council will accept to demonstrate compliance with these requirements? For example, would an online vehicle registration status report from TMR be sufficient, or is alternative documentation required?

We would appreciate your guidance to ensure our submission meets Council's requirements.

Thank you for your assistance.
publicQuestions.answer:
Good afternoon,

Thank you for your enquiry.

Council acknowledges that vehicle registration and Compulsory Third Party (CTP) insurance details in Queensland are administered electronically through the Queensland Department of Transport and Main Roads (TMR), and that physical registration certificates are not routinely issued.

For the purposes of Tender Schedule 5 – Insurance Details, Council will accept evidence of current vehicle registration status obtained from TMR as suitable evidence of compliance. This may include a current Vehicle Registration Status Check report or similar documentation generated through the TMR online services showing that the vehicle registration is current.

Tenderers should ensure that the information provided clearly identifies the vehicle and demonstrates that the registration is valid at the time of tender submission.

Should Council require any further verification during the evaluation process or contract period, additional supporting information may be requested.

Kind Regards,

LSC Procurement Team

publicQuestions.question:
Good afternoon,

I am currently preparing a tender response on behalf of Accelerated Training, a Registered Training Organisation (RTO 41474) based in New South Wales.

I am seeking clarification regarding Tender Schedule 6 – Local Content, specifically the criterion relating to the geographical location of the vendor and the requirement to provide evidence of an office within the Shire.

Accelerated Training is currently NSW-based; however, we are looking to expand our presence and service delivery into Queensland, having recently been successful in securing another tender opportunity within the state.

Could you please clarify whether having an established physical office within Livingstone Shire is a mandatory requirement for tender eligibility, or whether businesses based outside the Shire are still eligible to submit a tender response?

We would also appreciate clarification as to whether a business that is actively expanding its operations into Queensland, but has not yet established a permanent physical office within the Shire, would still be considered as part of the tender evaluation process.

We are keen to explore the opportunity to work with Livingstone Shire Council and would appreciate your guidance before finalising our submission.

Thank you for your time and assistance. I look forward to hearing from you.
publicQuestions.answer:
Submissions from businesses located outside the Shire are welcome and will be accepted for consideration. As outlined in the tender documentation, Local Content forms part of the evaluation criteria; however it represents a weighting of 10% of the overall assessment score.

Tender submissions will be evaluated against all criteria, with the majority of the assessment focused on the supplier's capability, experience, methodology and ability to deliver the required services.

title: PAH - Endoscopy Procedure Room Upgrade Project
description:
This procurement seeks to engage a suitability qualified Principal Contractor to deliver the PAH Endoscopy Procedure Room Upgrade Project within the existing Endoscopy Department at Princess Alexandra Hospital including full design and construction. The works involve the refurbishment and reconfiguration of existing departmental spaces, including the conversion of the current Dirty Utility, Staff Toilet, and adjacent shell office area into a dedicated endoscopy procedure room and associated supporting functions.

The scope includes completion of any remaining design development, construction, coordination and management of subcontractors, commissioning, defects management and handover within a live operational hospital environment. The project will deliver a contemporary procedure room designed to support complex endoscopy procedures and will include associated building and engineering services modifications such as:

•	Medical gases

•	Electrical service

•	ICT and communication infrastructure

•	Hydraulic services

•	Mechanical services and HVAC modifications

•	Nurse call and clinical systems

•	Radiation shielding requirements

•	Fire services modifications and compliance upgrades

•	Associated clinical infrastructure and room fit out.

The successful Contactor will be responsible for coordinating all aspects of project delivery, including stakeholder management, construction staging, commissioning activities, certification requirements, operational readiness and final handover.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
Metro South Hospital and Health Service (MSH) is a major provider of public health services, health education and research across Brisbane’s southside, Logan, Redlands, and Scenic Rim regions. MSH serves over 1.3 million people, representing approximately 24% of Queensland’s population, across a catchment of approximately 3,856 square kilometres.

MSH employs more than 22,000 staff and operates with an annual budget exceeding $4.2 billion. MSH comprises five major hospitals being Princess Alexandra Hospital, QEII Jubilee Hospital, Logan Hospital, Redland Hospital, and Beaudesert Hospital, supported by a growing network of community health centres.

Asset and Infrastructure Division (A&I) facilitate the delivery, management, and strategic forward planning of assets and infrastructure across MSH facilities. These services include a broad portfolio of essential work that enables staff to provide healthcare services to our communities including:

•	Real estate and land management and acquisition

•	Building refurbishment, expansions, and upgrades

•	Major building assets and mechanical equipment management and servicing

•	Strategic forward planning to meet healthcare demands and more.

This Procurement relates specifically to Princess Alexandra Hospital (PAH). PAH is a tertiary health care centre, providing care in all major adult specialties, apart from obstetrics. PAH is one of Australia’s leading academic and research health centres. PAH provides acute medical, surgical, mental health, cancer, rehabilitation, and allied health services. PAH is nationally recognised for the expertise in trauma management, and major transplantation centre for livers, kidneys, bone, cartilage, and corneas. PAH also does state-wide services including:

•	Queensland Adult Liver Transplant Service

•	Queensland Kidney Transplant Service

•	Queensland Tissue Bank

•	Donatelife

•	Queensland Spinal Cord Injury Service

The PAH Endoscopy Department provides a broad range of diagnostic and therapeutic endoscopy services. As clinical procedures continue to evolve, the department is undertaking increasingly complex interventional procedures requiring additional clinical space, specialised equipment and multidisciplinary clinical support.

A review of the existing Endoscopy Department identified that current procedure rooms have spatial and Infrastructure constraints that limit the safe and efficient delivery of complex endoscopic procedures. Existing room configurations present challenges associated with equipment positioning, staff movement, workflow efficiency and the accommodation of supporting clinical equipment required for procedures such as Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP).

title: BCEC Asset Capture & Condition Assessment
description:
SBC owns and operates the Brisbane Convention & Exhibition Centre (BCEC), one of Australia's premier convention, exhibition and events venues. The facility comprises a large and diverse asset portfolio supporting the delivery of world-class events and experiences, including building fabric, mechanical, electrical, hydraulic, fire, vertical transport and specialist operational assets.

To support effective asset management and long-term capital planning, SBC is seeking to establish a comprehensive and reliable understanding of the condition, performance and lifecycle of assets across the BCEC portfolio. This procurement will deliver an updated asset register, asset condition assessments, lifecycle modelling and renewal forecasts that will provide a robust evidence base for future maintenance, renewal and investment decisions.

The Services will be undertaken within a live operational environment. Respondents will be required to demonstrate an understanding of the challenges associated with working in complex facilities where business continuity, stakeholder engagement and minimising operational disruption are critical to project success.

The services are required to commence in December 2026 and are expected to run for approximately 20 weeks.

publicQuestions.question:
Hello, a few clarification questions:

1.	What is the approximate asset count, how many existing registers are there, and which recent assessments exist (for example roof or structure)?

2.	What is the requirement for specialist inspectors? Do they need to be registered engineers, and do they need trade-specific specialists for each asset class where a detailed engineering assessment is required?

3.	What are the event calendar and access windows over the Christmas and January period?

4.	Is the asset data collection limited to accessible assets only, or does it cover all assets?

5.	Is asset tagging required?

6.	Are we allowed to use the BCEC high-access equipment, or do we need to arrange our own where required?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. What is the approximate asset count, how many existing registers are there, and which recent assessments exist (for example roof or structure)? The complete asset population, quantities and completeness of existing asset registers, and the availability and currency of previous condition assessments have not yet been confirmed. These matters will be investigated during Stage 1 through a review of available asset registers, drawings, maintenance records, previous condition reports and other relevant documentation. Tenderers should allow for this review and validation as part of Stage 1 and clearly identify any assumptions in their submissions. Available records will be provided by SBC, subject to availability. The Stage 1 deliverable will include a validated understanding of the asset population, identified information gaps, and an agreed inspection strategy and Stage 2 price for approval before Stage 2 fieldwork commences.

2. What is the requirement for specialist inspectors? Do they need to be registered engineers, and do they need trade-specific specialists for each asset class where a detailed engineering assessment is required? Inspections must be undertaken by appropriately qualified and experienced personnel with competencies relevant to the asset class and assessment being performed. There is not a blanket requirement for every inspector to be a registered professional engineer. However, where an assessment requires engineering judgement, specialist technical expertise, or professional registration under applicable legislation or professional requirements, the relevant appropriately qualified and registered practitioner must be engaged. Tenderers should propose a suitably qualified multidisciplinary team, including relevant specialist engineering or technical disciplines for assets requiring detailed assessment. This may include, as applicable, structural, mechanical/HVAC, electrical, fire systems, hydraulic and vertical transport specialists. The need for specific specialists and the extent of their involvement will be developed through the Stage 1 Assessment Strategy and the Stage 2 rates and quantities.

3. What are the event calendar and access windows over the Christmas and January period? BCEC's event calendar and the associated access restrictions will be worked through during Stage 1. At a minimum, the Tenderer should assume unavailability of facilities and staff of SBC and BCEC from Thursday 24th December 2026 to Sunday 3rd January 2027. Tenderers should allow for the need to coordinate access with BCEC's operational and event requirements, including restrictions affecting event spaces, plant rooms, roof areas, back-of-house areas and other operationally sensitive locations. Access will be subject to SBC/BCEC approval and operational constraints, but adequate planning in Stage 1 should ensure consistent access for inspections throughout Stage 2. As part of their submission, Tenderers should identify any assumptions regarding access and working hours, explain how event-related constraints will be managed, and provide a program that accommodates access restrictions and reasonable contingency. The detailed access schedule will be coordinated with BCEC during mobilisation and program development.

4. Is the asset data collection limited to accessible assets only, or does it cover all assets? The objective is to account for the full asset population, rather than limiting the asset register and renewal forecast to assets that can be physically inspected. Physical inspection and data verification will be undertaken for the assets and quantities approved in the Stage 2 Inspection Plan, subject to safe and authorised access. Where an asset cannot be accessed or inspected, the limitation must be documented and the asset must still be accounted for through an appropriate approved treatment, such as existing-record adoption, age- or schedule-based forecasting, an agreed allowance, or a recommendation for further investigation.

5. Is asset tagging required? The current scope requires asset identification and a fit-for-purpose asset register, including asset IDs, descriptions, hierarchy and location information. Physical installation or replacement of asset tags is not identified as a mandatory requirement in the current scope. Any proposed physical tagging, labels, QR codes or other identification hardware will be considered by SBC and will be discussed during Stage 1. Physical tagging would only proceed if specifically approved by SBC/BCEC in Stage 1. Tenderers do not need to allow for tagging costs in their pricing, other than through hourly rates.

6. Are we allowed to use the BCEC high-access equipment, or do we need to arrange our own where required? The availability and permitted use of BCEC-owned high-access equipment would be confirmed in Stage 1, based on identified need through the Assessment Strategy. Submissions should state which equipment and access provisions are assumed to be supplied by BCEC and which are included in the Tenderer's rates or priced separately. Any use of BCEC equipment will be subject to confirmation of availability, suitability, operator competency, site requirements and SBC/BCEC approval.

publicQuestions.question:
Hi team, we have the following two queries please:

1. Are the inspections for stage 2 visual only or are respondents required to perform any further testing?

2. Are you looking for a new predictive modelling tool?

Thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Are the inspections for stage 2 visual only or are respondents required to perform any further testing? Stage 2 is not limited to visual inspections. Stage 1 will determine the exact methodology, but the approach will be risk and criticality based, with detailed physical and functional assessments sought for high criticality assets, visual inspections likely to be more appropriate for medium risk asset populations, and lower risk assets addressed through existing information, age-based or scheduled renewal forecasting where justified.

Specialist testing and non-destructive testing (NDT) are to be proposed where warranted by the asset type, available evidence, identified defects or risk. Such testing must be clearly identified and separately priced where applicable, and undertaken only where approved by SBC/BCEC. Stage 1 will establish the agreed approach, estimated quantities and price for approval.

2. Are you looking for a new predictive modelling tool? SBC welcome the use of modelling tools to conduct lifecycle modelling, though while we will remain open to adopting specific tools going forward, we do not want to be reliant on the use of specific tools beyond the duration of this engagement. The key outcome is that SBC has all of the modelling information, outputs, files, so that we can carry this information forward and further interrogate, refine, tweak over time.

The requirement is to develop an editable, fit-for-purpose asset lifecycle and renewal forecasting model that supports prioritised capital planning. The model is to use the agreed asset information, condition and remaining useful life estimates, criticality, replacement costs and documented assumptions to produce a prioritised 10-year renewal forecast, with the broader lifecycle outlook and scenario analysis required by the specification. The Tenderer may use/propose excel, PowerBI or more targeted modelling tools to develop and establish this model for SBC. The approach should be made clear in the proposal, as well as clearly outlining how this model and information will be transitioned to SBC for ongoing use beyond the duration of this engagement.

The model should support relevant scenarios, including unconstrained renewal needs, delivery within an assumed available budget, and the impact of deferring renewals. Tenderers should identify their proposed modelling approach and deliver the model in an accessible, editable format, including Excel where specified. Any proposed proprietary software or additional/ongoing licence costs must be clearly identified and are not to be assumed as a requirement.

publicQuestions.question:
Would Council consider a non-conforming tender that excludes BBQ cleaning, cleaning of fittings, fat-bucket emptying and fat-waste disposal from the Scope of Works, while fully including all scheduled electrical inspection, testing, functional verification, fault diagnosis, reactive maintenance, reporting and electrical repairs?

The proposed departure reflects a separation between specialist electrical services and general cleaning/waste-management services. publicQuestions.answer:
Council's primary requirement under this contract is the provision of electrical inspection, testing, functional verification, fault diagnosis, maintenance, reporting and repair services necessary to ensure the continued safe and reliable operation of public barbecue assets.

While BBQ cleaning, cleaning of fittings, fat-bucket emptying and fat-waste disposal are considered important elements of overall asset presentation and serviceability, Council has separate arrangements in place for routine park and facility cleaning. Accordingly, these activities are considered complementary to, but secondary to, the core electrical maintenance services being sought under this contract.

Council expects that, where cleaning-related issues are identified during the course of maintenance activities, reasonable actions may be undertaken to ensure the asset is left in a safe, serviceable and operational condition. Council considers this analogous to standard post-maintenance housekeeping and good asset stewardship.

Council will consider non-conforming submissions that exclude BBQ cleaning, cleaning of fittings, fat-bucket emptying and fat-waste disposal activities, provided the Respondent fully addresses the electrical inspection, testing, maintenance and repair requirements specified within the Scope of Works. Respondents should clearly identify any departures from the scope and detail any assumptions or exclusions within their submission.

Non-conforming submissions will be evaluated on their overall ability to meet Council's operational requirements, provide value for money and deliver a responsive and effective maintenance service.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
Metro South Health (MSH) is seeking information from the market on electronic register solutions to support the management of Schedule 8 (S8) and Monitored medicines across a Hospital and Health Service environment.

MSH currently uses paper-based registers in a range of settings, including wards, units, pharmacy, community services and correctional health. While these processes support current record-keeping requirements, they are labour-intensive, prone to manual error, difficult to audit, and do not provide real-time visibility of stock movements, balances or compliance issues.

MSH is interested in understanding whether suitable electronic solutions are available that could improve accuracy, security, reporting, auditability and workflow efficiency, while supporting compliance with Queensland legislative and policy requirements, including the Medicines and Poisons Act 2019 (Qld) and supporting regulations and standards.

This Request for Information (RFI) is for market sounding only and is not a commitment to purchase or proceed to a later procurement stage. Information gathered will help MSH understand product capability, implementation considerations, integration opportunities and indicative costs.

MSH is particularly interested in solutions that may be suitable across multiple sites and settings, and that can operate within a complex digital environment, including potential integration with systems such as Patient Administration System (HBCIS), Pharmacy Information System (iPharmacy), Electronic Medical Record (Oracle Millennium/ieMR, MetaVision), Automated Dispensing Cabinets (BD Pyxis ES) and other storage or pharmacy automation technologies.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes:
Vendors are invited to provide a concise written response outlining their product capability and suitability for MSH.

Please provide:

•	a brief overview of your organisation and proposed product, including product name, version, country of origin and support model

•	information on compliance with relevant Queensland legislation, standards and healthcare requirements

•	a summary of how the solution supports key workflows such as receipt, storage, transfer, administration, dispensing, stocktake, discrepancy management, disposal and patients’ own medicines

•	details of multi-site capability, scalability, user access controls, audit trails, reporting, data retention and export capability

•	information on integration capability with hospital systems, including Patient Administration System (HBCIS), Pharmacy Information System (iPharmacy), Electronic Medical Record (Oracle Millennium/ieMR, MetaVision), Automated Dispensing Cabinets (BD Pyxis ES), HL7 support, and any similar Australian implementations

•	ICT and hosting requirements, including whether the solution is cloud-based, on-premises, or hybrid; infrastructure and server requirements; storage and capacity requirements; network dependencies; backup and disaster recovery arrangements; and any third-party software or platform dependencies

•	cyber security information, including identity and access management, encryption, logging and monitoring, patching and update approach, anti-malware protections, remote access controls, incident response arrangements, and alignment with recognised security standards

•	a summary of implementation, training, maintenance and remote support arrangements

•	indicative pricing methodology, including whether pricing is based on users, stores, safes, transactions or another model

•	any brochures, case studies or data that support improve workflow efficiencies compared to manual registers

•	any brochures, technical documents or case studies that would assist MSH to understand the solution.

Responses should clearly identify standard functionality, optional functionality, assumptions, third-party dependencies and known limitations.

title: Emerald Sporting Fields Top Dressing
description:
Central Highlands Regional Council is seeking quotations from suitably qualified contractors to undertake sports field renovation works at nominated sporting fields within Emerald.

The works are intended to improve turf health, alleviate soil compaction, enhance drainage, improve playing surface quality, and support the long-term sustainability and safe use of community sporting facilities.

The successful contractor shall provide all labour, plant, equipment, materials and supervision necessary to undertake the following:

•	Hollow Tine Aeration (Coring) to relieve soil compaction and improve root zone performance. (All fields except McIndoe Field#3)

•	Collection, processing and management of extracted cores where required.

•	Supply and application of approved top dressing material.

Central Highlands Regional Council is seeking quotations from suitably qualified contractors to undertake sports field renovation works at nominated sporting fields within Emerald.

The works are intended to improve turf health, alleviate soil compaction, enhance drainage, improve playing surface quality, and support the long-term sustainability and safe use of community sporting facilities.

The successful contractor shall provide all labour, plant, equipment, materials and supervision necessary to undertake the following:

•	Hollow Tine Aeration (Coring) to relieve soil compaction and improve root zone performance. (All fields except McIndoe Field#3)

•	Collection, processing and management of extracted cores where required.

•	Supply and application of approved top dressing material.

•	Mechanical spreading and incorporation of top dressing to achieve a uniform surface finish of at least 10mm

•	Drag matting, brushing or similar finishing techniques to ensure even distribution of material.

•	Protection of existing turf, irrigation systems, drainage infrastructure and surrounding assets.

•	Removal and lawful disposal of waste materials generated during the works.

•	Site clean-up and reinstatement upon completion.

Topdressing material shall consist of a clean, washed, free-draining medium-coarse sand suitable for sports turf applications. The sand shall be free from clay, organic matter, weed seed, stones greater than 5 mm, and other materials. The Contractor shall nominate the proposed sand source and provide particle size distribution data upon request.

 The Contractor shall mechanically spread and incorporate topdressing material in incremental passes and shall not apply the full depth in a single pass. The material shall be distributed evenly across the nominated playing surface to achieve an average finished topdressing depth of 10 mm.

 Following each application pass, drag matting, brushing, levelling or other approved finishing methods shall be undertaken to ensure even distribution and incorporation of the material.

 Any low areas, depressions, hollows, birdbaths, surface undulations or other irregularities identified during the works shall be filled and levelled as required using additional topdressing material. Hand placement and finishing shall be undertaken where necessary to achieve a smooth, uniform playing surface and eliminate localised variations in surface level.

 Upon completion, the surface shall be free of ridges, windrows, excessive accumulations of material and abrupt level changes, and shall maintain positive surface drainage suitable for sports field use.

The Contractor is responsible for undertaking works in accordance with industry best practice, relevant workplace health and safety legislation, and manufacturer recommendations for all equipment used.

Works must be completed in a manner that minimises disruption to sporting clubs and facility users while maintaining safe access to surrounding areas. Any damage caused to Council assets during the works shall be rectified by the Contractor at no cost to Council.

Upon completion, the Contractor shall provide confirmation of:

•	Areas treated.

•	Aeration and coring methodology utilised.

•	Quantity and specification of top dressing material applied.

•	Any defects, irrigation faults or field condition issues identified during the works.

The completed surface must provide an even, safe and high-quality playing area suitable for community and competitive sporting use.

Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council is delivering a program of new social housing on Palm Island in collaboration with the Queensland Department of Housing and Public Works (DHPW).

Palm Island, also known as Great Palm Island, or by the Aboriginal name Bwgcolman, is the largest of twelve tropical Islands in the Palm Island Group. The settlement is named variously Palm Island, the Mission, Palm Island Settlement or Palm Community.

The group of Islands is less than 20 kilometres from the nearest point on the mainland (Lucinda) and is 65 kilometres north of Townsville over sea. The Islands are serviced by a 20 minute plane ride or one and a half hour ferry ride from Townsville and a one hour barge trip from Lucinda.

Palm Island consists of small bays, sandy beaches, fringing reefs, beautiful freshwater streams and steep forested mountains rising to the highest peak of 548 metres at Bentley Ridge. Other islands in the chain, such as Orpheus and North Palm have globally renowned resorts and marine research stations. Situated in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park, the surrounding reefs are as good as any on the outer reef, presenting wonderful fishing and diving opportunities and are used extensively by locals for hunting and gathering and other cultural purposes.

Palm Island is the largest discreet Indigenous community in Australia with approximately 4,000 people residing on Palm Island. There is high mobility between Palm Island and the mainland, and the population can increase to over 5,000 people during festivals and events. There are seven suburbs on the Island, running from Butler Bay in the south to Wallaby Point in the north, with the main, central settlement area, The Mission having the mall, shops, service centres, police station, motel, hospital and health service and Council chambers. Critical services infrastructure, including the Council’s works depots, waste and recycling facility, (Ergon) power station, water and sewer treatment plants, and two water supply reservoirs are at The Farm area, Solomon and Wallaby Point.

publicQuestions.answer:
1. Technical evidence and approvals

At tender submission, proponents should provide sufficient technical information to demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed system and its ability to meet the Principal's Requirements, including structural performance, cyclone resistance, durability, thermal performance, maintainability and applicable DHPW standards.

Detailed engineering, testing and statutory certification may be completed during the subsequent design development and approval stages, where appropriate. However, any proposed system must have a credible pathway to compliance, and the successful D&C contractor remains responsible for obtaining all necessary approvals and certifications before construction.

2. Limited application and compliant fallback

Council is open to considering innovative materials or construction systems as part of a conforming D&C proposal, including their limited application to suitable building components.

A fully compliant fallback solution may assist in managing delivery risk. However, any proposed alternative must be clearly identified and supported by sufficient technical evidence to enable its assessment. Council cannot provide advance acceptance of an untested or uncertified system, and any proposed solution would remain subject to the applicable design review, engineering and statutory approval requirements.

3. Mandatory site visit

The mandatory site visit requirement applies to the Tenderer submitting the D&C proposal. Where a specialist participates as a subcontractor or consultant to a Principal Contractor, the Principal Contractor's attendance will satisfy this requirement. Specialist participation in the site visit is encouraged where it would assist with understanding site conditions and delivery requirements.

4. Future demonstration or training opportunities

Council recognises the potential value of initiatives that develop local manufacturing, construction and maintenance capabilities.

Should participation in the current procurement be premature, you are welcome to submit a separate proposal for Council's consideration outside the current tender process. Any future demonstration or training initiative would be subject to Council's priorities, available funding, applicable approvals and procurement requirements.

The D&C scope includes removal of existing foundations, slabs, footings and other subsurface infrastructure to the extent necessary to accommodate the proposed subdivision infrastructure, earthworks and residential development.

Tenderers must also allow for the assessment and appropriate management of unsuitable material encountered during the works.

7. Demolition Waste Disposal

Palm Island does not have a landfill facility, only a Waste Transfer Facility.

The Principal Contractor is responsible for the removal and lawful disposal of all demolition waste on the mainland, including any hazardous materials, in accordance with applicable regulatory requirements.

All associated waste handling, loading, transport, barge freight and mainland disposal costs must be included in the lump-sum tender price.

8. Site Reinstatement

Council confirms that site reinstatement means removal of the existing camp infrastructure and preparation of the cleared site to accommodate the proposed subdivision earthworks and associated residential development.

The final site levels, grading, compaction and associated works must be coordinated with the subdivision civil design and applicable engineering requirements.

General

Tenderers must review the Reference Designs, supporting documentation, mandatory site inspection findings and relevant addenda, undertake any additional investigations considered necessary and include the required demolition and site preparation works within their Package 4 lump-sum tender price.

Any material assumptions, exclusions or proposed departures must be clearly identified in the tender submission.

publicQuestions.answer:

title: Commercial Development and Operation of Workers Accommodation Precinct – Palm Island
description:
Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council invites proposals from suitably qualified and financially capable organisations for the commercial development, establishment and operation of a Workers Accommodation Precinct on Palm Island, Queensland.

The precinct is intended to support Council's extensive capital works program and other construction, infrastructure and commercial activities anticipated on the island over the coming years.

Council seeks flexible, commercially sustainable proposals for accommodation facilities and associated infrastructure, potentially including furnished and air-conditioned accommodation, catering and dining facilities, recreational amenities, laundry, carparking, contractor laydown areas and essential services.

Proponents are encouraged to undertake their own market demand assessments and propose suitable accommodation capacity, development staging, investment arrangements and operating models.

Council's preferred arrangement involves a privately financed and operated facility, with the operator contracting directly with accommodation customers and paying Council rent for the use of the land. Proposals involving Council contributions towards enabling infrastructure may also be considered.

Initial accommodation operations are targeted to commence from April 2027. Council is progressing the Development Application separately, and the successful proponent will be required to coordinate with Council's planning consultants and undertake mobilisation activities concurrently with the approvals process.

Proponents are invited to propose commercially appropriate lease durations, renewal arrangements and rental structures. Consideration will also be given to the potential adaptability of the precinct for future hospitality and tourism accommodation purposes.

The proposed development site is located on Great Palm Island, Queensland, within an area endorsed by Council for this purpose.

Further project details, requirements and submission conditions are provided in the Invitation to Tender documents.

Tender closing date: Monday, 23 November 2026 at 2:00 pm AEST.

All formal tender enquiries and submissions must be made through VendorPanel.

vendorPanelDetails.background:
Palm Island Aboriginal Shire Council (Council) is progressing a substantial capital works program involving housing, roads, utilities, community infrastructure, tourism facilities and other developments. These projects, together with additional investments by government agencies and private developers, are expected to generate significant demand for temporary workforce accommodation on Palm Island.

Existing accommodation facilities have limited capacity to support the anticipated construction activity. Council therefore intends to facilitate the establishment of a commercially operated Workers Accommodation Precinct.

Site and land arrangements

The proposed precinct is located within the Town Area defined under the Palm Island Improved Future Land Practices Indigenous Land Use Agreement (2010). The site has been endorsed by the elected Council, which has confirmed its authority to grant the relevant land interest.

The successful proponent will be expected to enter into an appropriate commercial land tenure arrangement with Council, with the lease duration, renewal arrangements and rental structure to be determined through the procurement and negotiation process.

Planning and development coordination

Council is independently progressing the Development Application through Milford Planning and Langtree Consulting Engineers.

Proponents must ensure their proposed accommodation concepts, layouts, infrastructure requirements and staging arrangements are compatible with the overarching planning and development approval process.

The successful proponent will be required to liaise with Council's appointed consultants and progress mobilisation activities concurrently with the Development Application, targeting initial accommodation operations from April 2027, subject to statutory approvals.

Accommodation and infrastructure requirements

The precinct should provide safe, comfortable, appropriately serviced accommodation suited to Palm Island's remote location and tropical climate.

Proponents should consider accommodation configurations, catering and dining facilities, recreational amenities, laundry, parking, contractor laydown areas, utilities, wastewater management, cyclone resilience, accessibility and other operational requirements.

Accommodation capacity, development staging and infrastructure solutions are intentionally not prescribed. Proponents are expected to assess the market independently and propose commercially viable solutions capable of responding to demand over time.

Commercial considerations

Council prefers privately financed development and operations, with accommodation customers contracting directly with the operator and the operator assuming commercial occupancy risk.

Council contributions towards enabling infrastructure may be proposed where justified. All proposals must include land rental consideration payable to Council.

The potential for future conversion to hospitality and tourism accommodation is desirable but is not a mandatory requirement.

Proponents should refer to the Invitation to Tender documentation, indicative site plan and capital works information for further details.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes:
Council seeks a commercially sustainable, professionally managed Workers Accommodation Precinct that supports the delivery of Palm Island's substantial capital works program while generating long-term economic and community benefits.

Desired Outcomes

Establish operational workforce accommodation from April 2027, with capacity and subsequent expansion determined by demonstrated market demand.

Deliver safe, comfortable, cyclone-resilient and appropriately serviced accommodation suited to Palm Island's remote tropical environment.

Provide suitable supporting facilities, including full catering and dining services, recreational amenities, laundry, parking, contractor laydown areas and essential infrastructure.

Encourage private sector investment, with proponents independently assessing demand, securing customers and managing commercial occupancy risk.

Establish a financially sustainable arrangement that generates ongoing land rental income for Council.

Enable progressive infrastructure development and expansion in response to construction activity and other accommodation opportunities on the island.

Support local employment, training, Indigenous business participation and economic development.

Desirable Features (Non-Mandatory)

Private ensuite rooms or self-contained accommodation units.

Flexible modular infrastructure that can be relocated, expanded or reconfigured.

High-quality recreational facilities, including a gym and communal spaces.

Energy-efficient design, renewable energy solutions and sustainable water and wastewater management.

Accommodation and facilities adaptable for future hospitality and tourism operations.

Commercial proposals that minimise Council's financial contribution while providing attractive long-term lease returns.

Conditions and Performance Expectations

The successful proponent will be expected to:

Coordinate closely with Council, Milford Planning and Langtree Consulting Engineers throughout planning, design and mobilisation.

Maintain a realistic implementation programme targeting operational readiness from April 2027.

Comply with applicable planning, building, work health and safety, environmental, cultural heritage and operational requirements.

Maintain appropriate insurances, licences, certifications and documented management systems.

Provide effective facilities management, maintenance, housekeeping, catering, security and emergency response arrangements.

Maintain transparent accommodation tariffs, booking arrangements and agreed mechanisms for future price adjustments.

Meet agreed standards for accommodation availability, cleanliness, maintenance, catering quality, customer service and incident response.

Provide regular performance reporting covering occupancy, accommodation capacity, operational performance, maintenance, safety and agreed community benefits.

Maintain the leased land and facilities in good condition and comply with agreed end-of-lease and site handback obligations.

Key Project Benefits

The project is expected to strengthen Palm Island's capacity to deliver major infrastructure and housing investments, reduce accommodation constraints affecting construction contractors, attract private investment, generate rental revenue for Council and create local employment and business opportunities.

Council also recognises the potential longer-term value of infrastructure that could support hospitality and tourism activities following the peak construction period.

Council welcomes innovative proposals and alternative commercial arrangements, provided they demonstrate financial viability, credible delivery capability, appropriate risk allocation and measurable benefits to Palm Island and its community.

Proponents should refer to Parts A, B, C and D of the Invitation to Tender for the detailed requirements, proposed commercial framework and return schedules.

Located in the heart of Western Sydney and in one of the fastest growing areas of New South Wales, the Diocese of Parramatta comprises 80 vibrant and dynamic school communities that stretch from Dundas Valley, north to Richmond, west to Katoomba and south to Luddenham.

There are 58 primary schools and 24 secondary schools and two trade pathway campuses supporting approximately 46,000 students and almost 5,000 staff.

Parish priests, principals and school communities work together to provide faith-filled, radically inclusive and caring environments that allow young people to grow in their faith and better understand the mission of the Church. This is achieved through religious education, faith formation, liturgical celebrations, sacramental programs, pastoral care and support.

Under the pastoral leadership of the Bishop of Parramatta, the Most Reverend Vincent Long Van Nguyen OFM Conv DD, students and staff are encouraged to reach out to those most in need.

The purpose of this RFT is to solicit a suitably qualified vendor to provide canteen services for Caroline Chisholm College, Glenmore Park. The canteen services (breakfast, recess and lunch) will be provided to students during school days (Monday -Friday only) and will have healthy food options and affordable prices. The canteen license is to commence in Term 1 2027 for a term of two years (with an option to renew for a further 1 year).

publicQuestions.question:
Hello,

We are reviewing the Oaky Creek tender and would appreciate Council’s assistance with a few clarifications:

Is there a mandatory pre-tender site meeting?

What is the required project completion date?

Could Council please confirm whether the project is design and construct or construct only? Item 1.04 includes the preparation of detailed drawings, while the Bridge Knowledge design report appears to indicate that detailed drawings have already been prepared. Are further drawings available, and are tenderers required to engage Bridge Knowledge for any remaining design work?

Given that detailed design drawings and certification are included under item 1.04, could Council please confirm whether professional indemnity insurance is required and, if so, the minimum level of cover?

Are tenderers required to adopt the design nominated by Bridge Knowledge, or would Council consider an alternative design that meets the project requirements?

Thanks and warm regards
publicQuestions.answer:
1. A non-mandatory site meeting is scheduled for 10am on 29 October 2026

2. Required by June 2027. General Conditions of Contract – Contract Information Item 13

3. The Bridge Knowledge detailed design has been based on a propriety “off the shelf” prefabricated steel and concrete bridge. The tender has been written on the basis that tenderers will likely nominate their preferred low-cost bridge solution and this will likely require some amendment to the provided detailed design to meet the project requirements such as waterway area and road approach levels.

4. Not required. General Conditions of Contract – Contract Information Item 24

5. The tender has been written on the basis that tenderers will nominate their preferred low-cost bridge solution. Each bid will be assessed on its respective merits against the project requirements.

publicQuestions.question:
Will the Council accept a documented and implemented Corporate WHS Management System without ISO 45001, AS/NZS 4801 or OFSC accreditation?

Will an internally audited Environmental Management System be accepted without ISO 14001 certification or an independent audit report?

Can the Council confirm the contractual completion period, including allowance for bridge fabrication and Fisheries Permit approval?
publicQuestions.answer:
1. Council will assess each management system on its merits in the tender assessment process. Whilst those systems that do not have current 3rd party accreditation will score lower in the tender assessment than those systems that do have accreditation, tenders will be assessed using a weighted scoring process where the ratio of price to non-price criteria will be 60:40 and the scoring of management systems is only one of the 4 non-price criteria being considered. Conditions of Tendering 7.1 – Evaluation of Tenders

2. As above

3. June 2027. General Conditions of Contract – Contract Information – Item 13

publicQuestions.question: Do we need to price the confirming price schedule provided if we propose an alternative design?
publicQuestions.answer:
Whilst the tender offer requested is Lump Sum (Section 1 of Tender Schedule) for either conforming or alternative tenders, Council has only requested a Schedule of Prices (Section 2 of Tender Schedule) to assist in valuing completed work for the purposes of progress payments and consequently the Schedule of Prices should be considered as information only.

Council is expecting contractors to tender details of their preferred bridge solution, which may be different in configuration and materials to the undetailed bridge structural concept shown in the engineering design drawings. Council will assess each tender on merit, providing the submitted tender meets the functional intent expressed in the tender documents.”

publicQuestions.question:
Could you please clarify the following:

1. In respect to the Break-up of Lump Sums, Item 1.04 requests an amount for Engineering Certification. As the Bridge Knowledge Drawings are IFC, does this mean that 3rd party certification is required?

2. On the IFC drawings it shows approximately 90m of roadworks. From the site meeting council advised that minimal roadworks is required. What would be expected length required?

3. Item 9.02 in the Break-up of Lump Sums requires an amount for the install of gabion baskets. At the site meeting it was noted that no gabion baskets are required. Could you please confirm that this is correct.

Thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
1. The Engineering Certification requested relates to the bridge structure itself as the design drawings do not detail or specify any structural aspect of the bridge itself, only the approaches and the abutment pile details. As the tenderer is expected to nominate their preferred low-cost bridge solution, it is expected the tenderer will provide Engineering Certification to confirm their nominated solution meets the appropriate Australian Standards such as AS4100, AS5100 etc. It is for this reason the issued design drawing has been marked “Issued For Tender” to indicate that further information is required.

2. Whilst the “Issued For Tender” drawings show a 90m long transition on eastern approach to the new bridge, this is indicative only and does not indicate the Limit of Contract. The tenderer would only be required to extend the transition to a sufficient distance to match the existing road approaches, commensurate with the likely low traffic speeds at this location. However, the transition distance would be expected to increase if there is say an increase in the height of the deck of the proposed bridge structure from that shown in the tender drawings to ensure the transition is safe for traffic.

3. Any Break-up of Lump Sum items that are not applicable to the bid, should have a zero shown in the associated Unit Rate and Sub-Total cells to indicate this

Darling Downs Hospital and Health Service invites offers for the provision of design services and the provision of construction services of the resulting works for the Texas Multipurpose Health Service, Primary Healthcare Clinic Project, in accordance with the requirements of this Request for Offer.

The purpose of this Request for Offer is to obtain fixed lump sum pricing for Separable Portion A, to design the Primary Healthcare Clinic and an indicative estimate only for Separable Portion B, the construction.

Value for money will be determined by reference to the demonstrated capability of offerors in delivering similar projects, their capacity to complete the construction before the 30th of June 2028 and other factors as set out in Request for Offer documentation.

Darling Downs Health provides exceptional patient-centred care to approximately 300,000
people living in a catchment spanning 90,000 square kilometres. The catchment extends
north to Taroom and Murgon, south to Texas, east to Toowoomba, and west to Goondiwindi and Miles.

Our public hospital and healthcare services comprise 30 facilities, including a large regional
referral hospital, an extended inpatient mental health service, three medium-sized regional
hub hospitals, 11 rural hospitals, four multipurpose health services, a primary health care
clinic, a community care unit, two general practices, and six residential aged care facilities.
As one of the largest health employers in regional Queensland, our services are delivered
with the support of a workforce of over 7,300 people.
vendorPanelDetails.queryCutoffAtRaw: Monday 16 November 2026 02:00 PM (E. Australia Standard Time)
vendorPanelDetails.background:
The Texas Multipurpose Health Service (MPHS) Primary Healthcare Upgrades Project will improve the functionality, capacity and operational efficiency of the existing health service facility to better support current and future healthcare needs within the Texas community. The project includes the establishment of a new General Practitioner (GP) clinic within the existing hospital site, together with targeted refurbishment, reconfiguration and minor extensions to address identified clinical, administrative, staff amenity, security and storage deficiencies.

Establishing the GP clinic within the hospital site will provide opportunities for greater integration between primary and hospital-based healthcare services. The GP clinic will be able to utilise relevant existing hospital infrastructure and support facilities, including pathology and other shared clinical services, reducing the need to duplicate facilities and improving coordination between primary and acute care.

Texas MPHS is experiencing increasing demand for emergency and aged-care services. The proposed upgrades will therefore also improve the facility's capacity and functionality to support these priority service areas, including improvements to Emergency Department patient flow and triage, aged-care storage and supporting facilities, and associated staff and patient amenities.

The project will make efficient use of the existing building footprint by repurposing and reconfiguring existing spaces wherever practicable, supplemented by targeted new works where additional capacity is required. Key improvements include accommodation for the new GP clinic, improved administration and clinical support areas, additional staff and patient amenities, enhanced storage, establishment of an Emergency Department triage function, and improved security at the Community Health reception.

The works will be planned and delivered with consideration of the ongoing operation of Texas MPHS and the need to maintain safe and functional healthcare services throughout construction. The project will seek to minimise disruption to clinical and support services while delivering durable, compliant and fit-for-purpose outcomes.
