title: Wildlife Detection Technology
description:
Request for Information (RFI) – TMRICTRFI26178 Wildlife Detection Technology.

TMR is seeking information on available and emerging solutions that support a range of capabilities associated with wildlife management in road environments. The capabilities are divided into four core pillars: Detection, Identification, Monitoring and Alerting. At a high level, TMR is interested in identifying technologies that can fully or partially support the four pillars:

1. the automated detection of wildlife near the State Road Network.

2. automated wildlife classification and identification. (accurate identification of wildlife species)

3. automated monitoring of wildlife road-crossing activity and/or in proximity to road infrastructure.

4. the automated generation of real-time alerts/notifications/warnings when wildlife is detected on or near road environments/corridors, together with reporting and analytics to support driver awareness.
buyer: Department of Transport and Main Roads - ITB

vendorPanelDetails.buyerAddress:
532 Beams Rd
Carseldine, Queensland 4034
Australia
vendorPanelDetails.buyerDescription: The Department of Transport and Main Roads provides reliable, resilient and responsive transport networks and digital services that are safe and accessible for everyone. This procurement is led by TMR's Information Technology branch (ITB).
vendorPanelDetails.queryCutoffAtRaw: Thursday 29 October 2026 04:00 PM (E. Australia Standard Time)
vendorPanelDetails.background:
Wildlife–vehicle collisions are an ongoing challenge across road networks and can present safety risks to road users, contribute to wildlife injury and mortality, and create operational, maintenance and environmental management impacts.

While static wildlife warning signs are deployed across parts of the State Road Network to warn drivers to the potential presence of wildlife, their effectiveness in influencing driver behaviour or reducing collision incidents may be limited.

As part of its ongoing commitment to improving road safety outcomes and exploring innovative approaches to network management, TMR is investigating the current state of wildlife detection and driver warning technologies. Advances in sensing, monitoring, communications and artificial intelligence technologies may provide opportunities to improve the real-time detection of wildlife on or near roads and support more targeted warnings to drivers.
vendorPanelDetails.desiredOutcomes: Through this market engagement, TMR aims to better understand the range of technologies currently available, emerging industry capabilities, and potential future applications that may assist in addressing wildlife-vehicle collision risks across the transport network.

publicQuestions.question:
Could Council please clarify the following requirements under Attachment C of the Technical Specification:

1. RPEQ Certification: Can Council confirm that structural and mechanical engineering designs must be certified by appropriately registered RPEQs in their respective disciplines?

2. 30% Design Review: Is the four-week Council review period mandatory, or can approval be provided earlier?

3. 80% Design Review: Is a separate four-week review period required following the 80% design submission, including the review workshop and resolution of comments?

4. IFC Design Review: Is an additional four-week Council review period required following submission of the final IFC drawings, before fabrication can commence?

5. Project Completion: Considering the engineering approval requirements and subsequent fabrication, installation and commissioning works, does the nominated completion date of 28 May 2027 remain unchanged?

6. Alternative Completion Date: Would Council accept a justified alternative completion date, and would such a tender remain conforming for evaluation purposes?
publicQuestions.answer:
Council confirms that the structural and mechanical engineering designs must be undertaken and certified by appropriately registered RPEQs in their respective disciplines.

Tenderers must allow a four-week Council review period following submission of the 30% design. Council will endeavor to complete its review earlier; however, the submitted program must allow the full four-week period.

Yes. A separate four-week Council review period must be allowed following submission of the 80% design. This period includes the review workshop, Council’s comments and resolution of those comments.

Yes. Tenderers must allow an additional four-week Council review period following submission of the final Issued for Construction (IFC) drawings. Council anticipates minimal comments at this stage, provided the comments arising from the 80% design review have been satisfactorily addressed.

Fabrication may only commence once Council has approved the IFC drawings.

28 May 2027 remains the nominated completion date in the tender documentation. However, Council will consider a revised completion date supported by a realistic program that allows for the required design reviews and subsequent fabrication, installation and commissioning works.

Tenderers are requested to submit both of the following programs, identifying the proposed completion date for each:

1.	A program allowing four weeks for each Council review at the 30%, 80% and IFC design stages, totaling 12 weeks of Council review time.

2.	An alternative program allowing two weeks for each Council review at the same design stages.

The two-week review option is to be provided for Council’s consideration and does not constitute a commitment by Council to the shorter review periods.

Yes. Council will consider a justified alternative completion date where the submitted program is realistic and reflects the works required, including design, Council reviews, fabrication, installation and commissioning.

A tender proposing an alternative completion date on this basis will remain conforming for evaluation purposes. Tenderers must provide the four week Council review programs described above, clearly identifying the proposed completion dates and supporting assumptions.

publicQuestions.answer:
Question. Is it possible to get minutes of the tender briefing, for anyone who may have missed it? or is it possible for there to be another?

Answer - PowerPoint presentation that was delivered during the tender briefing will be uploaded as an addendum shortly.

No formal minutes of the briefing were taken. The session was intended as an informal opportunity to provide an overview of the tender requirements and answer general questions from potential respondents.

As discussed during the briefing, Council is seeking feedback on the three proposed pricing models included within the tender documentation. While respondents are requested to provide pricing against each model, Council intends to adopt only one pricing model following evaluation of the responses. Alternative options can be submitted for Council to consider.

The session also provided an opportunity to discuss Council's objectives in relation to achieving a fair and consistent approach to work allocation and pricing across the panel arrangement under the new contract.

Respondents should refer to the tender documentation for all requirements, including eligibility criteria and evaluation details.

Reg. the pricing response schedule, detailed pricing schedule;

Question- top note states "Unless expressly stated, rates are deemed to include labour, supervision, plant, ordinary travel",

Answer – Your response should clearly identify any pricing elements that are excluded from your rates. Unless expressly stated otherwise, Council will assume that all quoted rates include labour, supervision, plant, and ordinary travel.

Question- section 1, a to g, indicates block sizes at standard site, is section 3 then added to this, regardless of what the top note states?

- what defines a standard site?

Answer – A standard site is considered to be a flat block of land with reasonable site access and no unusual constraints. Where additional allowances or services are included under Section 3, these should be priced separately as specified. Unless expressly stated otherwise, Council will assess pricing based on the inclusions and assumptions outlined in the pricing schedule.

Question-what defines heavy vegitation? (wet vs dry? principals representative? height of vegitation?)

Answer – For the purposes of pricing, respondents should define in the Trigger/Evidence section what they consider to be "Heavy Vegetation" and the assumptions underpinning their rates, including factors such as vegetation density, height, accessibility, and any other relevant site constraints. Council will evaluate pricing based on the definitions and assumptions provided by each respondent.

Question-what defines slopped site? (above x degree incline? a property that has levelled areas, but an embankment on it?)

Answer – Sloped Site has not been prescribed by Council. Respondents are requested to define in the Trigger/Evidence section what they consider to be a Sloped Site for the purposes of their pricing and clearly state any assumptions that apply (e.g. incline, extent of slope across the site, access constraints, or other relevant factors).

Question- what is regarded as urgent response? is it same day, 3 day ?

Answer – For the purposes of this tender, an Urgent Response is considered attendance or commencement of services within 24 to 48 hours of Council providing notice. Respondents should base their pricing on this response timeframe and or any clarifications you would like Council to adopt should your submission be successful.

Question- What is the difference between above urgent response, and emergency response/after hours or are these the same?

Answer – For the purposes of this tender, an Urgent Response is generally considered attendance or commencement of services within 24 to 48 hours of Council providing notice. An Emergency / After Hours Response refers to an unplanned incident requiring immediate attendance outside normal business hours, such as a natural disaster, public safety risk, infrastructure failure, or other event requiring prompt rectification.

Respondents should clearly define any response time assumptions that underpin their pricing and service offering.

Question - what is the set standard of deliverable? is it based on height of cut, or princiapals reprisentative descretion?

Answer – Council has not prescribed a specific standard of deliverable for the purposes of this tender. Respondents should clearly state the assumptions underpinning their pricing, including any proposed standards such as cut height, site presentation outcomes, or quality measures. The proposed methodology and deliverables will form part of Council's evaluation and may be further refined with the successful panel members during contract finalisation.

Question- is the after hours and emergency charges in section 2 and 3 combined, or both added seperately to the standard block size?

Answer – Respondents should clearly identify where each rate applies and how it is intended to be applied. If an After Hours or Emergency rate is proposed in addition to a standard block size rate, this should be clearly stated. Council will assess the applicability and methodology of the proposed rates as part of the evaluation.

Question- what defines the included area in section 3? is it townsville's landlocked council, devistions or x km from the city centre?

Answer – For the purposes of this contract, the applicable area is the Townsville Local Government Area (LGA). Respondents should base their pricing on service delivery within the Townsville LGA and clearly identify any assumptions or limitations that apply to their rates.

Question .scope of work responsibility matrix indicates supplier for site inspection and preperation, does this indicate that supplier can access site to view in full prior to completion date?

Answer – Site inspections will be arranged by Council in consultation with the panel member. Where there is a significant delay between the initial inspection and the commencement of works, the contractor may request a further site inspection.

Respondents should note that site conditions may not always be fully apparent during an inspection, particularly where access or visibility constraints exist. As part of their submission, respondents should clearly identify how unforeseen site conditions will be managed, including any proposed variation mechanism, rates, or charges that may apply where additional work is identified during the delivery of the services. Any variations would be subject to Council approval onsite at the time of the works.

publicQuestions.answer:
If you do not wish to participate under the Rate Card pricing methodology, please clearly state this in your response by leaving the pricing schedule blank and advise that you would only be interested in providing pricing on a site-by-site basis when services are requested.

The Rate Card pricing is being sought to enable Council to assess whether this approach represents the best value and operational fit for the contract. While the contract is primarily intended for overgrown allotment services, a Rate Card arrangement may also provide Council with the flexibility to engage panel suppliers to support operational resource shortages, where required.

Council will initially evaluate responses against Stage 1 and Stage 2 requirements, including Local Benefits, Insurances, Capability and Experience. Shortlisted Respondents will then progress to the pricing evaluation stage, where Council will further assess the proposed pricing models and determine the most suitable commercial approach for the contract.

Council acknowledges that Respondents may apply different assumptions, inclusions and methodologies when developing their pricing submissions. Accordingly, Respondents should clearly identify all assumptions, definitions, inclusions and exclusions that underpin their proposed pricing. These details will form part of Council's overall evaluation, including methodology, capability, commercial offering and value for money.

The final engagement and pricing model will not be determined until the completion of the evaluation process. However, Respondents should note that choosing not to provide pricing may impact their ability to progress to the final stage of the evaluation.

Hourly rate card quote - this is the response in "RFt schdule 3, response schedule, detailed pricing pricing schedule tab: heading 3. LABOUR, PLANT AND DISPOSAL RATES"?

We want to ensure we can respond to each of the 3 proposed pricing structures clearly. without a clear line in the document where one starts/finishes or individual tabs, is the above correct in assuming these are the different pricing options for response?

thank you
publicQuestions.answer:
Schedule 3 – Detailed Pricing Schedule

1. Base Rate by Property Size

The Base Rate should represent your fixed rate to deliver the required mowing or clearing service for the relevant property size. The rate should clearly identify all inclusions, assumptions and any exclusions applicable to the service.

2. Site Conditions and Response Adjustments

This section should identify any proposed adjustment to the Base Rate where site conditions differ from a standard site. Adjustments should clearly describe the circumstances in which the additional rate would apply.

3. Labour, Plant and Disposal Rates

This section should detail the hourly rates applicable for labour, plant, equipment and disposal services. These rates may be utilised where:

•	Council engages/adopts services on an hourly rate basis; or

•	Additional works are required beyond the agreed Base Rate and are approved by Council's Representative; or

•	Site conditions or circumstances not reasonably identifiable during the initial site inspection result in additional time or resources being required to complete the works. These additional charges would be discussed and agreed with Council's Representative at time of works should additional works be agreed to the hourly rates would then be applied.

•	Council may use this for other operational requirements across Council as required

Items 1 and 2 would form part of a single rate card.

Item 3 could be offered as a standalone option, where Council would request that you review the site, provide the estimated number of hours required, and Council would apply your nominated hourly rate. Alternatively, Item 3 could be incorporated into Items 1 and 2 as a variation mechanism where additional works are required.

As previously advised, Council is exploring all available options to develop a pricing model that works for both the Contractor and Council, and these are some of the scenarios that may be considered during evaluation.

Alternatively, if you have a different pricing approach that you believe would provide a better outcome, we encourage you to include it in the Alternative Pricing Proposal tab for Council's consideration.

publicQuestions.question:
1. Does Council remove or manage contamination levels in FOGO and GO before it is transported to the final processing facility?

2. What level of contamination (i.e. 2% by mass) does Council consider to be deemed as "ordinary contamination".

3. Does Council have any specified days that it would like to deliver FOGO and GO?

4. What definition or classification does Council use for Processed product? e.g. does it need to meet AS4454 criteria or other specification?
publicQuestions.answer:
Q1. Does Council remove or manage contamination levels in FOGO and GO before it is transported to the final processing facility?

A1. No. Council does not undertake pre-processing or contamination removal of FOGO or GO prior to delivery to the processing facility. Material is delivered as collected, and the Service Provider is responsible for monitoring contamination levels, managing contamination, processing the material, and disposing of any contamination or residual waste in accordance with the Contract requirements.

Council's waste collection contractor does, however, undertake a fortnightly bin audit program. During these audits, staff visually inspect up to 60 FOGO bins per fortnight for contamination. Where contamination is estimated to exceed 10% of the bin contents, the bin is not collected, and educational material is provided to the resident. Where contamination is estimated to be less than 10% of a bins content, the bin is collected and tagged with an educational notice identifying the incorrect materials observed.

________________________________________

Q2. What level of contamination (i.e. 2% by mass) does Council consider to be deemed as "ordinary contamination"?

A2. Council has not prescribed a specific contamination threshold or percentage for ordinary contamination. Tenderers are required to propose contamination thresholds, measurement methodologies, and management procedures as part of their tender submission for Council's review and approval. Ordinary contamination is expected to be managed by the Service Provider as part of the contracted processing services. Prohibited or hazardous waste is treated separately under the Contract. For information, Council's household organics bin audit undertaken by Ann Price Consulting in May 2026 estimated the average contamination rate within Ballina Shire household organic bins to be approximately 3.9%. This figure is provided as historical performance information only and is not intended to represent a contractual contamination threshold.

________________________________________

Q3. Does Council have any specified days that it would like to deliver FOGO and GO?

A3. Council has not specified particular delivery days for FOGO or GO deliveries. However, the RFT requires the processing facility to be available to receive Delivered Material during the minimum operating hours specified in the tender documentation.

For information, Council aims to collect and deliver a relatively consistent quantity of material across each weekday to support the efficient operation of its collection services and transport resources. Tenderers should therefore anticipate regular weekday deliveries, with delivery volumes generally distributed as evenly as practicable throughout the week.

The minimum receival hours specified in the RFT are:

•	Monday to Friday: 7:00am to 3:30pm

•	Weekends and Public Holidays: 9:00am to 2:00pm

Council's expectation is that the facility will be capable of accepting Delivered Material during these times.

________________________________________

Q4. What definition or classification does Council use for Processed Product? For example, does it need to meet AS4454 criteria or another specification?

A4. Processed Product is defined as any product recovered from or produced using the Delivered Material during the provision of the Services. Processed Product must comply with AS 4454-2012 Compost, Soil Conditioners and Mulches where applicable. The Service Provider must also comply with all relevant NSW EPA requirements, including any applicable Resource Recovery Orders, Exemptions, and the Compost Order in force at the time.

This project aims to upgrade the system to provide a reliable, efficient and sustainable irrigation solution that will support year-round use, enhance turf quality, reduce operational costs and align with Council’s standards for quality public facilities.

publicQuestions.question:
Council has listed RRJ PVC pipe from 80 to 200mm. Can we use 80 & 100mm SWJ pipe downstram of the control valve ?

Can we install a flow meter downstram of the filter for flow monitoring ? There is not on the pump shed drawings / If so would council prefer magflow or a mechanical flow meter ?

Is the filter backflush mechanism hyddraulically driven or electrically driven ?

Council specifies that services need to me manually potholes. Can they be HydroVaced ?

Do sprinkler laterals need to be sand bedded ?

Do the all pipe collars need to be raised off the trech floor as specified ?? Even 25, 40 & 50mm pipes ?? This is an overkill

Council specifes in the 90day warranty period that material that are damaged throgh vandelism and theft are to be replaced at the contrcors expensive !! Are you for real ??

Council specifies 2.5mm cable in the tender. You can acheive valve closure up to 3km's with 2.1mm. Can we use 2.1mm ??

Can we specify another Control System other than Galcon GSI. MRCC uses Hunter. Can I quote Hunter ??
publicQuestions.answer:
Dear Tenderer

Please find the below replies.

1. Council has listed RRJ PVC pipe from 80 to 200mm. Can we use 80 & 100mm SWJ pipe downstream of the control valve ?

No. Council requires Rubber Ring Joint (RRJ) PVC pipe to be maintained as specified for all lines from 80mm to 200mm, including downstream of the control valves. Swan Hill soils are prone to seasonal movement, shifting, and thermal expansion/contraction. RRJ provides the necessary joint flexibility to prevent catastrophic cracking under sports ovals, whereas SWJ creates a rigid line vulnerable to ground shear.

2. Can we install a flow meter downstream of the filter for flow monitoring ? There is not on the pump shed drawings / If so would council prefer magflow or a mechanical flow meter ?

Yes, a flow meter is highly desirable. Please install it downstream of the filter in the pump shed. Council prefers an electromagnetic flow meter (magflow) rather than a mechanical meter. Magflow meters have no moving parts, meaning lower long-term maintenance, zero pressure drop across the device, and superior accuracy when handling raw or slightly turbid water typical of irrigation reserves.

3. Is the filter backflush mechanism hydraulically driven or electrically driven?

The backflush mechanism itself is hydraulically driven (using the system's internal water pressure via hydraulic valves to reverse the flow), but it is initiated by an electrical signal/controller (usually a 24V AC or DC pulse trigger via a differential pressure switch or timer). Tenderers must ensure the design accommodates electrical control wiring back to the main cabinet.

4. Council specifies that services need to me manually potholes. Can they be HydroVaced ?

We prefer manual potholing, however, using Hydrovac may be considered as long as due care is taken not to disturb the existing assets. Requested to mention both the options in your quote, if possible.

5. Do sprinkler laterals need to be sand bedded ?

Yes, all sprinkler laterals must be sand bedded. To protect the PVC lines from localized damage and friction leaks caused by sharp clay clods or stones during trench backfilling and future soil compaction, a minimum 75mm to 100mm sand envelope (bedding and overlay) is required. Relying on native site backfill for lateral lines is not approved.

6. Do the all pipe collars need to be raised off the trench floor as specified ?? Even 25, 40 & 50mm pipes ?

Yes, this rule applies across all specified sizes. Raising the collars/sockets off the trench floor ensures that the pipe barrel rests evenly on a continuous underlay of compacted bedding sand rather than bridging across high spots. This avoids localized point-loading stress on the joints once the trench is backfilled and heavy turf-maintenance machinery runs over the ovals.

7. Council specifies in the 90 day warranty period that material that are damaged through vandalism and theft are to be replaced at the contractors' expense.

Please ignore the vandalism and theft part.

8. Council specifies 2.5mm cable in the tender. You can achieve valve closure up to 3km's with 2.1mm. Can we use 2.1mm??

No. Please adhere strictly to the 2.5mm² cable specification. While 2.1mm² cable may achieve valve closure mathematically up to 3km under perfect conditions, Council specifies 2.5mm² to account for standard electrical degradation, voltage drop under heavy simultaneous multi-valve operations, and future network expansions. Sticking to 2.5mm² ensures system reliability and fits Council's regional maintenance compatibility requirements.

9. Can we specify another Control System other than Galcon GSI. MRCC uses Hunter. Can I quote Hunter??

Council prefers sticking to the specifications. However, please feel free to quote for alternatives as well.

publicQuestions.answer:

Hope this answers your queries.

publicQuestions.question:
Can you clarify what sort of quick coupling valve is require on the oval ? Is this a turf valve ? What Size do you require ?

Did you want scour valves located at the ends on the 150mm maiinline. We can install a 50mm ball valve with a camlock fitting. ?
publicQuestions.answer:
Hi Tenderer,

Please find the reply below:

•	Quick Coupling Valve: Council requires a 25mm (1") heavy-duty brass quick coupling valve with a resilient rubber turf cover, installed exactly flush with the final turf surface for manual cricket pitch irrigation.

•	Scour Valves: Yes, scour valves are required at the terminal low points of the mainline networks to enable high-velocity flushing and full system drainage.

•	Fitting Approval: The proposed 50mm ball valve with a male camlock fitting is approved for scouring purposes. It must be housed in a commercial-grade, lockable valve box supported by treated pine sleepers and a 20mm crushed rock drainage base as per the typical drawing details.

Thank you

publicQuestions.question:
Clarification – PVC trench widths and depths

Could Council please confirm the trench width and minimum pipe cover requirements for all PVC pipework, including the DN200 mainline from the pump station to the irrigation valves and all smaller pipes down to DN25, including sprinkler submains and laterals?

The PVC detail on Sheet 3 specifies a minimum trench width of the pipe outside diameter plus 200 mm, allowing 100 mm clearance each side. Does this apply to every pipe size, or would narrower trenches be accepted for smaller pipes where the required bedding, support and compaction can be achieved? If permitted, please specify the minimum widths.

The 600 mm minimum cover is shown on the HDPE/RCP details, while the PVC detail only dimensions 50 mm minimum bedding below the pipe and 150 mm protective embedment above it. Please confirm whether 600 mm cover also applies to all PVC pipe sizes, or specify the minimum cover permitted for mainlines, submains and laterals, including any increased requirements at road, driveway or access-track crossings.

For clarity, please state cover as the distance from finished ground level to the top of the pipe, rather than total trench excavation depth.
publicQuestions.answer:
•	Mainlines (DN80 to DN200): The strict rule of pipe outside diameter (OD) plus 200mm minimum trench width must be maintained for all primary lines. This provides a mandatory 100mm of side-support clearance on each side of the pipe to allow proper compaction of the sand envelope and to visually inspect the Rubber Ring Joints (RRJ).

•	Smaller Lines (DN25 to DN50): For the smaller sub-mains and sprinkler laterals (DN25, DN40, DN50), a narrower trench width is acceptable down to a minimum of the pipe OD plus 100mm (50mm clearance on each side). This variance is strictly conditional on the contractor demonstrating void-free side-support tamping and a complete sand embedment zone around the pipe barrel.

Minimum pipe cover is defined as the distance from the finished ground surface level to the top crown of the pipe barrel. To protect the lines from Swan Hill's highly seasonal clay shifting and aggressive turf care machinery (such as deep spiking and coring), the following cover schedule applies:

•	Mainlines (DN80 to DN200): 600mm minimum cover across all zones.

•	Submains & Laterals (DN25 to DN50): 450mm minimum cover within sports fields and established garden boundaries.

•	Roads, Driveways, and Vehicle Access Tracks: 750mm minimum cover is required across all pipe sizes. If existing underground utilities prevent achieving a 750mm depth at a crossing, the pipeline must be retrofitted through a heavy-duty protective conduit sleeve with a minimum of 450mm cover.

title: Mayne Yard ELP Sheds Fire System Upgrade
description:
Queensland Rail is undertaking the Mayne Yard Electric Locomotive Provisioning (ELP) Sheds Fire Systems Upgrade at Mayne Yard, Bowen Hills. The ELP Sheds form part of Queensland Rail’s major maintenance and stabling facility, which operates 24 hours a day, seven days a week and supports rail operations across the Southeast Queensland network.

The project involves upgrading the existing fire protection systems across the seven ELP buildings, comprising L, M, N, O, O1, P and Q Blocks. The works include replacement and upgrade of dry fire detection and alarm systems, emergency warning systems, smoke extraction and associated communications, cabling and infrastructure, together with testing, commissioning and handover.

The works are required to be delivered within a live operational rail environment, with Mayne Yard remaining operational during construction. This creates significant staging, access, isolation and operational interface requirements, including coordination with maintenance activities and rail movements.

To manage these constraints, the works are structured into Separable Portion 1 (SP1) for development and validation of the delivery methodology, access, staging, isolation requirements, detailed programming and stakeholder coordination, followed by Separable Portion 2 (SP2) (optional) for supply, installation, testing and commissioning of the works.
